madam president, the question of the cultivation of gmos and their possible prohibition in the individual member states has long been a subject of passionate debate in this field. certainly, the numerous profit-making lobby groups have a share of the blame. and profit is what's at stake here, in my opinion, first and foremost. the last time this was shown was at the end of last year, when the committee on the environment, public health and food safety voted on the committee's recommendations for the second reading. many controversial amendments passed by only one vote. gmos are a danger both to the environment itself, to the genetic pool and to species diversity, and above all to human and animal health. i would point out that most of the impact studies on gmos have always been funded primarily by multinational corporations, led by their lobbyists. the harm of gmos to human health is not even mentioned in public discourse, yet we already know about them from independent studies. i must say that i am very disappointed with the current state of the text presented. the european parliament went into the negotiations with a very good text which we could and should have defended, but we failed to do so. therefore, i personally refuse to support the current version of the proposal in any way. we have to stop gmos in the european union.
in writing. the member states of the european union have long called for the adaptation of existing legislation to allow them greater freedom and flexibility in restricting or prohibiting the cultivation of genetically modified organisms on their territory. however, negotiations were blocked by the member states themselves for four years, and the resulting compromise proposal of the council, adopted by 28 environment ministers in july 2014, was far from perfect. however, during the debate in the european parliament, the text was significantly improved, particularly in terms of weakening the powers of companies seeking to market gmos in the eu, in favour of member state governments. it was also essential to strengthen the measures required by member states to ensure the coexistence of the crops grown and, in particular, to prevent cross-border contamination. overall, this is a good compromise that helps to protect europe's biodiversity and preserve natural habitats and ecosystems, among other things. however, as vice-president of the envi committee, i would like to see a text that reflects even more the public opinion in europe, which is increasingly turning against gmos, and in particular their presence in food. the debate between pro- and anti-gmo groups is not over, and we look forward to the steps taken by commission president jean-claude juncker, who has committed to strengthening the democratic process on gmo authorisation in europe and ensuring that research on gmos is truly independent.
in writing. the new protocol to the fisheries partnership agreement concluded by the european commission and the democratic republic of são tomé and príncipe in may 2014 builds upon the previous protocol which expired in 2014. the new proposal was signed to achieve two main objectives: on the one hand, to allow eu vessels to fish within the limits of available surplus in são toméan waters, but at the same time to allow the eu to promote and monitor the effective implementation of a more responsible tuna fisheries policy, as defined by the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas. i fully support the deepening of cooperation between the eu and this former portuguese colony, which is an important partner for the eu, not least from a geopolitical point of view. the inhumane way tuna is caught is a major global problem and the european union should do its utmost to ensure that the funds it spends on its fisheries policy are always allocated to sustainable fishing. this should also apply to the case of this protocol, which should ensure more targeted financial interventions, in particular towards strengthening control mechanisms in the fight against illegal fishing.
madam president, i welcome this decision, i supported it. i supported it for two reasons, firstly because it is always good to give the national states the possibility of regulating a matter by their own legislation where european regulation is not necessarily necessary. and this is precisely the case where european adjustment is not necessarily necessary. secondly, in the european union, there is in some countries, in my view, an unjustified and, in some cases, even anti-scientific hysteria against genetically modified crops. i do not take his views from anyone, if ever a country wants to ban the cultivation of genetically modified crops, please do so, but do not force other countries to follow suit. i am glad that this decision, i hope, will unblock the possibility of such a veto at the level of the european union.
i have supported this proposal, madam president, because i believe that it will soon give the member states of the european union the instrument, in the form of a new directive, to enable them to regulate the cultivation of genetically modified organisms in their territory effectively. states will now be free to restrict, restrict or even ban authorised gmos. this changes the existing situation, which was governed by the 2001 directive, under which gmos were in principle authorised centrally for the whole of the european union and only a reporting obligation existed for the national authorities. the european food safety authority will continue to assess only the risks of gmo cultivation. i therefore regard today's decision as the fulfilment of the principle of subsidiarity, which is often spoken of but not always respected at european level.
in writing. i am not afraid of genetically modified maize, but i believe that member states should have the right to allow or not to allow the cultivation of gmos on their territory. i am voting for this amendment so that there is no blocking of authorizations at eu level if there are member states which do not want genetically modified crops on their territory.
in writing. the proposal to allow member states to restrict the cultivation of gmos on their territory is a compromise that could correct the current ambiguity in this area. it is also positive that the way in which decisions are made in europe about the safety and use of gmos in our agriculture is not called into question and that the position of efsa is not weakened. unfortunately, i think that such a broad and easy option for countries to ban the use of gmos on the basis not of scientific but of political reasons is wrong. it constitutes a certain weakening of the principle of the single market and may serve as a precedent for other similar decisions. moreover, given the benefits of using gmo techniques in a number of areas, i consider it to be not very functional and potentially leading to further problematic decisions. these negatives to me outweighed the benefits of the proposal, and that's why i didn't support it.

mr president, this debate today is a kind of déjà vu, it is not new, we have already experienced it here, we experienced it here a few years ago and there were the same objections back then, which were based on the lobbying materials of the data processors. there was a threat of price increases even then. we've only been partially successful, and in the meantime, there's been a whole series of food fraud scandals and a significant decline in consumer confidence. that's the result. now, the results of the european consumer association survey show that more than 90% of the respondents want the origin of the meat to be clearly indicated. consumers not only welcome such information on the packaging, but are rather surprised that it has not been there for a long time, because they do not understand why processed meat should not be subject to the same strict and quality regulations as unprocessed meat. this is regardless of how the rules are enforced in the member state concerned. we are not talking about any small quantity of meat, in some eu countries up to half of all meat products are without any indication of origin as a result of this situation, and this is alarming in my view. there's so much lobbying going on right now, so much fear of price increases and bureaucracy, that i feel like this debate is really in the right place, and it has to show, among other things, who they listen to first, consumers or industry. we're voting on whether the commission should work on the proposal, not on the legislation itself. why would anyone want to kill the discussion in the first place? in writing. 90% of european consumers want to know the origin of the meat ingredients in processed foods. the data is based on the statements of a number of consumer organisations, but also on a survey carried out by the commission. the origin of meat is generally of paramount importance to eu consumers. some producers have therefore opted for the indication of the origin of meat on a voluntary basis, while others do not provide this information to consumers, arguing that the indication of the origin of meat in processed food could lead to an increase in the price of the final product of 1550%. on the contrary, surveys of consumer organisations have quantified the estimated average price increases in cent units. i believe that increasing the transparency and clarity of information can help to restore european consumers' confidence in the european food market. at the same time, however, it is important to ensure that the increase in information on food packaging does not have a negative impact on the availability of these products. given the wide variation in the data on the possible impact on the final price of the products, does the commission have a precise cost analysis for the mandatory introduction of the indication of the origin of the meat in processed products?
i feel it is my duty to ensure that the european union guarantees the quality and safety of foodstuffs through legislation. if i thought that the mandatory indication of the origin of the meat ingredients in processed foods would improve their quality, i would certainly vote in favour of the motion for a resolution. even if it means a higher price. i don't think that's what it is. who among us today can claim that meat from one country or another guarantees quality? i'm sure none of us would dare say it that way. the reasons for the indication of the origin of meat in meat products which have been raised here today, such as the possibility of choice, knowledge of origin, monitoring of the whole production and distribution chain, are all legitimate interests and reasons which can mean greater comfort for the consumer. however, they should not be a reason to impose a new obligation on each manufacturer. as you know, many producers are already taking advantage of this consumer interest by offering to add the indication of origin of the meat components as a supplementary standard to their products. thus, any consumer can already choose a manufacturer who can offer him this superior standard. in the context of competitive advantage, there will certainly be more. however, i see my responsibility in ensuring and promoting quality for every consumer and it has no direct link with the place of origin.

in writing. anti-dumping and anti-subsidy measures affect approximately 0,25% of all imports into the eu and are often the only way the eu can protect its industries from the damage caused by unfair dumping practices by companies from non-eu countries. anti-dumping and anti-subsidy instruments need to be adjusted to better protect eu trade, provide a stable base for businesses and protect industries. codification of council regulation (ec) no 1515/2001 of 23 july 2001 on the measures that the union may take following a report adopted by the wto dispute settlement body on anti-dumping and anti-subsidy matters could, in my view, be useful.
in writing. i see the common import rules primarily as safeguard measures designed to prevent possible critical situations, for example where certain products are imported in such increased quantities and under such conditions that they cause injury to the union industry. the european union's common commercial policy, backed up by appropriate legislation, is necessary in this case. in the interests of clarity and transparency of union law, i therefore welcome the codification of council regulation (ec) no 260/2009 on common rules for imports.
in writing. the common commercial policy is also an important part of the concept of the common market. the common export rules are governed by the principle of free export as a standard, which states that no quantitative restrictions are applied to exports from the european union (eu) to non-eu countries. however, it could be that, as a result of unusual market developments, the eu will need to take safeguard measures to prevent a possible critical situation arising from a shortage of basic products, to allow for the correction of such a situation or to fulfil international commitments taken by the eu or by all eu countries, in particular in the area of trade in basic products. in such a case, it is necessary to codify the common rules.

in writing. — i am pleased that the european parliament has supported this comprehensive resolution on counter-terrorism, which considers the root causes of radicalisation and terrorism and pushes for the implementation and review of existing eu measures. we need action both at home, across the eu and an external strategy to ensure a holistic approach to fighting terrorism.
although the european parliament is permeated by actors with different national interests and different ideological views, i believe it is important that we can agree on certain issues across the political spectrum. i regard the question of combating terrorism as one of them. however, the joint motion for a resolution did not include the two groups, the greens and the gue/ngl. i find it sad that the demands of the two groups have not been incorporated so that the european parliament has a genuinely common acceptable proposal. the proposal does not emphasize the social factors of the whole problem as i would consider appropriate. for example, an amendment that pointed out that poverty, unemployment, and a lack of prospects for full integration into society can lead to individuals needing destructive behavior that adversely affects society as a whole was not passed. i believe that to have a debate about radicalism without a comprehensive focus on the social problems of society will not lead to the desired goal. focusing on the consequence rather than the cause has fatal consequences in all social issues, and is especially dangerous when it happens in issues that threaten the lives of citizens both in europe and around the world. the proposal thus often focuses on how to obtain information on european citizens and how to monitor them in the most effective way. i believe that approach is wrong and that is why i did not approve the motion for a resolution.
the subject matter of the resolution before us is one of the most pressing security issues of our time. i believe that we must stress as much as possible that the effectiveness of counter-terrorism policy requires a change in the foreign policy of some member states of the european union. it is necessary to assess the consequences of actions such as the bombing of libya or the support of anti-government forces in syria. the joint resolution unfortunately does not reflect the need for a self-critical approach that could help to improve counter-terrorism policy, but also to understand why illegal immigration to europe is increasing. the residual colonial thinking in some metropolises, the non-conceptual aid to developing countries which, for example, helps more the marketing of our agricultural surpluses than the development of agriculture in the receiving states, the uncontrolled export of arms to unstable areas - these are just some of the activities that contribute to the rise of terrorism and the breakdown of states. the concept of the european union's mediterranean partnership, as well as the relationship with the african union, is outdated. it does not reflect the dramatic changes in europe and in the mena countries, the middle east and north africa. but these ideas are completely absent from the motion for a resolution on which we are voting. i could not therefore support its contents and voted against it.
i support this resolution unequivocally in all its points. i strongly and categorically condemn all terrorist attacks, the promotion of terrorism, the celebration of persons involved in it, and the advocacy of extremist violent ideologies, wherever they occur or are advocated in the world. i consider extremist and terrorist groups to be the greatest threat in the world today, which cannot be eliminated 100%, but i am convinced that a comprehensive approach can significantly improve the security of the population. it is necessary to adopt a 'multilingual approach' to combating terrorism, not tackling it at the moment of planned attacks, but addressing the root causes of radicalisation leading to violent extremism in a comprehensive way, for example by strengthening social cohesion and inclusive societies and political and religious tolerance, by preventing social exclusion. the internet and its monitoring will increasingly play an essential role in preventing recruitment, terrorist propaganda and, not least, the illicit arms trade. however, the european union cannot implement any effective strategy without intensive cooperation with other states - not just those where terrorist organisations are concentrated - because terrorism knows no borders and neither can increased eu border controls be a solution in themselves.
in writing. discussions about terrorism often draw hasty conclusions and offer hasty solutions to the consequences, not the causes. i therefore welcome the fact that this resolution stresses the need to focus on combating the roots of terrorism. it is necessary to invest in education, to promote integration, social inclusion, dialogue, mutual tolerance and understanding between different cultures and religions. like freedom of expression, these values are the foundations of european civilization and the european union must not trade them for a closed-door approach and a false promise of security. i therefore welcome the fact that the resolution excludes proposals to suspend the schengen system. i agree that terrorism must be fought at all levels - national, european and global. that is why i supported the final version of the resolution.
i supported the resolution on counter-terrorism measures in question, since it contains, among other things, many measures which propose not only addressing the consequences but also addressing the causes of the situation. but i believe that we must take great care not to take any well-intentioned action that would lower the standard we have worked together to build in the eu. when we mention the possibility of temporarily introducing document checks in the context of schengen cooperation, we should proceed at the internal border consistently with the possibilities provided by the schengen borders code and avoid a situation where checks in the border territory of individual member states (e.g. document checks) are carried out in such a way that their effect is equivalent to the effect of carrying out border checks. in this context, the judgment of the court of justice in joined cases c-188/10 and c-189/10 can be mentioned.
in writing. — i voted in favour of the joint resolution on the fight against terrorism. one month after the paris attacks, this text is of high importance. among other points, it calls for a better approach to tackle radicalisation but also to prevent recruitment and departures to join terrorist organisations. the text also stresses the need to fight against financial support to terrorist organisations and trafficking of firearms. this resolution calls on the member states to prevent the movement of terrorist suspects by strengthening external border checks. with this vote, the european parliament also came to agreement on a deadline of the end of 2015 for finalising the european pnr system and urges the council to make faster progress on the data protection package in order that talks on the eu pnr directive and the data protection legislative package can proceed in parallel.
in writing. i supported the joint motion for a resolution on the extension of the mandate of the internet governance forum (igf). the igf is a crucial platform that can continue to advocate for principles such as the openness and accessibility of the internet to all and net neutrality. these are also the principles on which the eu is building its digital single market. the demand for the protection of personal data, intellectual property, copyright and the protection of children in the digital environment from exploitation on the internet (whether through social networks, games, advertising or inappropriate content) is coming to the fore. there are still large gaps in this area. the european union must be actively involved in the solution, as it does not provide adequate protection in this area. internet governance must respect children's rights to protect their identity, to their healthy mental and physical development. it is therefore appropriate that the mandate of the igf be extended by the un general assembly and that the eu continue to promote the principles of openness, net neutrality and security within the igf.
in writing. — i voted in favour of the resolution calling on the united nations to renew the mandate of the internet governance forum. the igf has so far successfully brought together stakeholders for discussions, but more should be done to improve this forum. i count on the commission which will be participating on behalf of the european union to work in this direction.
mr president, i would sign every sentence that my predecessor, mr hayes, of my group, has said here. i did not take the view of my group and voted for the text approved by the envi committee. i agree with the committee's call for legislation to introduce mandatory country of origin labelling for meat and processed food. and i don't think that maintaining the principle of voluntariness is the right solution. only a negligible proportion of producers and processors voluntarily provide information on the origin of the ingredients of foodstuffs. consumer confidence in food is thus at a very low level and the mandatory indication of origin could increase it. surveys carried out by the european consumer organisation, confirming the findings of the european commission, show that 70% of eu citizens consider information on the country of origin of food and even 90% of eu citizens consider information on the country of origin of meat to be very important. the adoption of the legislation requested by the envi committee is also supported by czech consumer protection organisations, which is why i am in favour of mandatory labelling, also because i am a member of the agri committee.
mr president, i have long been in favour of labelling products and of indicating their composition. but for each legal standard we must ask whether european consumers need it and what the implications will be. i think it's going to have two impacts, both on the producer and the consumer. in both cases, this will only have the effect of increasing the price of the final product. i therefore supported the position of the european people's party, which supports the labelling of the origin of meat in processed foods only on a voluntary basis. we believe that eu legislation must have limits and that not every meat has to be a library or a store of information.
in writing. — i voted against the resolution on mandatory origin labelling. i note that there are a significant number of reports and analysis which suggest that should mandatory origin labelling be brought in, it would add extra burdens on our smes, while at the same time giving a limited result in terms of added value.
in writing. i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the indication of the country of origin of meat ingredients in processed foods. firstly, because it is not a legislative proposal at the moment, but merely a call to the european commission to look further into the issue, including an assessment of all the implications for consumers, traders and producers. there should be a public debate on this issue, whatever the outcome. i shall then base my position on a possible legislative proposal on a detailed study of them.
in writing. european consumers have been rightly angered on several occasions in recent years by meat suppliers who have withheld information on the origin of goods in order to increase their profits. i believe it is time that the european consumer is given all the relevant information before buying meat to help him make a truly informed decision. the european union can help in this respect and i think it is right that it should put the interests of consumers ahead of those of suppliers who refuse to treat their customers honestly. consumer organisations have been calling for meat labelling for several years and the reasons why they should not be complied with run counter to the interests of citizens who are not asking for much. they demand the right to information about the food they consume. i do not think that these demands are unreasonable or excessive. i would consider it unwise, on the contrary, to deny the public the right to know the origin of the meat they consume and to hide behind pseudo-arguments that are used by record companies that refuse to tell their customers the whole truth about their products. i therefore feel it is my duty to vote in favour of a proposal which will help consumers to become more market-oriented.
in writing. i'm all for people buying quality products. i do not agree, however, with the central control of the packaging, labels and other indications of products. all these measures simply increase the cost of production and do not respect the fact that some people would rather buy at a lower price than pay more for detailed labeling. people themselves as consumers determine which companies they trust and from which products they buy. if they do not trust companies that do not label meat in a satisfactory way and buy only from companies that label products according to the ideas of consumers, then a natural self-regulation of the market will occur. companies with poor labelling will lose profits, or even lose market share, or have to improve their labelling. but i am strongly in favour of the customer being free to choose whether he wants a lower price or a more detailed marking.
in writing. i did not support the meat labeling resolution in processed foods, even though some of the public are calling for it. i hope the commission will give careful consideration to this. our analysis indicates that there are considerable difficulties in implementing this requirement, that it would lead to considerable problems in practice and, in particular, that it would entail considerable costs. they'd be carried by consumers. it is also clear that no regulation is going to prevent the fraud that has occurred in this area. for similar agreements, a balance of benefits and costs must always be considered. the fact that some members of the public or interest groups support regulation is not a sufficient reason for it to be established. for this reason, i do not think that this regulation is appropriate and that is why i did not support it.
in writing. i am of the opinion that country of origin labelling is a useful and desirable measure for single-component foods such as all types of meat, eggs, milk, fruit or vegetables where traceability of the country of origin is not a problem. i am in favour of introducing general requirements for transparent labelling of the origin of foodstuffs, provided that this has a real impact on consumer awareness and, above all, on the quality of the products that consumers buy. i do not share the view that mandatory labelling of the origin of meat in processed meat products can in itself be a preventive measure, as was the case with the horse meat scandal. thorough checks by the relevant control authorities of the member states are no substitute for labels. for the reasons stated above, i voted against the european parliament resolution because i do not believe that the proposed measures will lead to an increase in the quality of the products. on the contrary, they will certainly lead to price increases, which i do not consider to be a deliberate 'smart regulation' and consumers certainly do not want it to be. i am, however, in favour of voluntary labelling of origin for processed food, even if it leads to higher prices for some producers, because in this case the consumer will be able to choose for himself, as is already the case for organic foodstuffs.
in writing. i am for effective consumer protection, not unnecessary regulation. i therefore support the country of origin labelling of fresh, chilled and frozen meat, as required by the commission regulation which will come into force in april this year. it can guarantee that the origin of a particular piece of meat is clearly indicated from the producer to the consumer. the european parliament voted today to call for mandatory country of origin labelling of meat ingredients also for processed foods. however, increasing bureaucracy and burdening even the smallest producers will not ensure a higher quality of meat products. for us consumers, quality control and enforcement are more important. the introduction of mandatory labelling of the origin of meat for individual product components, such as sausage in pizza, entails increased costs for producers, which are reflected in the increased price of meat products for the final consumer. moreover, the information obtained is not relevant for the quality of the product. it may be interesting, but it's not necessary for quality assurance. it would only be if we accepted that a different origin of meat automatically implies a different quality. some producers already routinely indicate the country of origin of meat in meat products where consumers so request. that is why i voted for voluntary labelling of processed foods. however, this motion was not passed, and i did not vote for the final form of the resolution.
in writing. i voted against today's vote because i believe that a sufficient level of consumer awareness can be achieved without imposing an obligation to indicate on a product not only the country of origin but also, for example, the city of origin of the raw material used. i consider that, in the context of the possible influence on the final price of the product, it is sufficient to indicate only the country of origin.
in writing. i voted against the ep resolution on the indication of the country of origin of meat ingredients in processed foods. the resolution calls, inter alia, for the european commission to submit a report and subsequent legislative proposals making the indication of the origin of meat in processed foods compulsory. in practice, this measure would mean that the country of origin and the country where the individual meat components were processed would be indicated on the product. this would disproportionately increase the administrative burden and costs for processed food producers and would make the labelling of products even less clear and the product ultimately more expensive for consumers. these effects would be particularly pronounced in the case of products made from several types of meat (e.g. salami). however much i can imagine that there will be an increase in administrative burden in justified cases, i cannot vote for a proposal where this burden is not offset by a proportionate benefit for consumers. the proposal is in that category. i am therefore in favour of keeping the labelling of the origin of meat in processed products on a voluntary basis, as is the case up to now.

in writing. on 10 march 2015, i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on interchange fees for card-based payment transactions. this directly applicable regulation should lead to a duplication of fees charged by banks to merchants for processing card payments across the eu. and it was timely, as interchange fees for card payments are not transparent and vary widely between eu member states. this was to prevent merchants and customers from being robbed by unreasonably high fees that served only to accumulate huge profits for the banks that issued the card. this ceiling, which will apply to both cross-border and domestic payments, should ultimately lead to a reduction in the costs of payment card users and create a level playing field for payments across europe. since both traders and buyers should benefit from the lower charges, i decided to support this regulation in my vote.
in writing. the eu remains convinced that it can eliminate customer costs and force companies to provide something for nothing. the cap on card transaction fees may lead to a reduction in the number of banks offering free account maintenance according to some reports, similar changes in the us were the main reason why banks did just that. in addition, the banking sector will have to introduce a cross-subsidy for payment terminals if it cannot charge a corresponding price for the operation of this element of the payment system. this will make it harder to finance new innovations such as contactless payments. it's because competition is suppressing rather than promoting it. that is why i voted against this motion. the european union would do better to stop burdening small businesses, including small banks, with disproportionate regulation.
in writing. the regulation of interchange fees for card payments is far from certain to achieve its intended purpose of reducing the price of goods or services for end-users. it deals with only part of card payments, which is linked to the complicated system that finances and develops cashless payments. the main chance is that the trend of card usage growth will ensure that the increased use of payment cards compensates for the decrease in the price per transaction and the development of cashless payments will not stop. the main reason for supporting the regulation for me was the situation where, as a result of the disputes that had taken place between the commission and the card companies, an opaque environment was created that would make the regulation transparent. failure to adopt the regulation would preserve the status quo, which would probably be worse. however, rather than direct regulation, i would welcome more transparency of fees, especially in view of the relatively high costs for small businesses to accept payment cards. but regulation is unlikely to improve their situation.

‒ the situation in the euro area has a major impact on the economies of all eu countries and must therefore be closely monitored and evaluated. in particular, the czech republic has expressed its support for adopting the euro in the medium term. the european parliament's report analyses in detail the ecb's actions over the past year, both in the area of fiscal and monetary policy. from a financial perspective, 2013 was not an ideal year, with the euro area continuing to decline or stagnate in all major indicators. unemployment in the euro area rose to 12% (around 25% in some countries), euro area gdp fell by 0.4% and inflation continued to decline, with some countries approaching zero or reversing deflation. this trend is dangerous in terms of the ability of the most indebted countries to comply with debt relief schemes. unfortunately, the ecb's 2013 projections did not anticipate the current combination of stagnating growth and very low inflation, and we need to take a more cautious approach to the current projections of stronger economic growth and higher inflation in 2015 and 2016. the ecb also needs to re-analyze the conditions for access to credit by smes, as the credit enhancement measures put in place by the ecb have not proved successful. on financial stability, i welcome the fact that the single supervisory mechanism (ssm) has become fully operational.

answering the question posed by raising the blue card. i do not think that the european union, if it is to function, should not have the means. it is very important that the european union, if it is to be a strong association of states, has its own finances and its own financial policy. i think your question is a good one, but it's being directed in the wrong direction, towards me. i am a federalist and i want a strong europe.
the report before us is full of information about fraud and the misuse of european money. because it's taxpayers' money, it's obviously a very serious matter. i am only concerned that the european commission and probably the majority of the european parliament refuse to see the cause of these problems. the reason is precisely the fatal presumption that money must be redistributed in this way through the european union. why can't the money stay in the hands of the state to pay for the roads? why can't they stay in the council's coffers and pay for the sidewalks? why can't they stay in people's pockets so that people can decide for themselves how to invest in their hotels and so on? that's why i say, let's cut the funding and that'll cut the corruption.
at the moment, in my view, further enlargement of the union is not realistic. however, the countries with which we are negotiating possible accession should be given a clear signal that the possibility still exists. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the european union is able to take part in the negotiations on the future of the european union. of the group of countries seeking to join the european union, montenegro is, in my opinion, the most active in the negotiations. according to available and comparable criteria, at least. it is also an exaggeration to say that montenegro even uses the euro as its currency, but without a corresponding agreement with the european union. despite the apparent progress, a number of serious problems remain, notably the implementation of the basic rules of the rule of law, the more effective reduction of corruption or the prevention of the link between the public administration and crime. our common task is to help our montenegrin friends to solve these problems, and thus to open a more realistic chance for eventual entry.
for the gue/ngl group. i would like to stress that serbia is the central economy of the balkans and without the stabilisation of serbia it is not possible to stabilise the balkan countries as a whole. i would also like to stress that this country will need macro-financial assistance because it has the largest number of refugees on its territory in the whole territory, 700 000. also, there's been flooding that's flooded some of the mines, so serbia has to import coal today. i think it is also important to help serbia to build up its renewable energy capacity. there's been a lot of progress in terms of hydroelectric power, but i think there's a lot of reserves and it could be a promising area for neighboring countries. i would also like to emphasise that we should appreciate serbia's progress in judicial reform, in administrative reform and also in the fight against corruption, even though there are some reservations, which were finally mentioned here. i think it's a country that deserves our attention, and it's also important that we help to tap the potential that's there for the entire region.
in writing. i believe that the coordination of economic policies is essential for the eu's economic growth, and i would therefore like to call on the member states to cooperate more closely, and i would like to see this cooperation intensified between the european parliament and the national parliaments. i would also like to call for a review of the mff by the new parliament, thus giving it new political legitimacy. i would like to mention two long-standing problems with the eu budget. one of them is the failure to respect the principle of budgetary accuracy, which applies to the eu budget as it does to all national budgets. if we as the eu want to be an example, we must respect this principle. there is no way that the commitments we have made are not covered by sufficient funds. and the second issue that's troubling the eu is tax evasion. by failing to address this problem in the long term, our budgets are losing significant resources. i would like to express my great confidence in the newly established special committee of the european parliament to deal with unfair tax practices. i believe his work will be very useful.
in writing. ‒ i am in favour of this regulation on common rules for imports from certain third countries: setting rules for imports, based on uniform principles across the eu, and setting simple and identical formalities to be carried out by importers will boost trade with third countries. i support the provision on surveillance and safeguard measures adopted by the commission: the text provides the commission with the necessary tools to investigate and ensure eu interests are not endangered, while avoiding unnecessary administrative burdens on importers.
in writing. on 11 march 2015, the european parliament debated the report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on certain procedures for applying the stabilisation and association agreement between the ec and its member states, of the one part, and the republic of montenegro, of the other part. i abstained from voting on this codification for several reasons. first of all, the positive developments and reforms that montenegro has already undertaken on its way to deeper european integration should be commended. in my opinion, montenegro is on a very good path to becoming a full member of the eu in the near future. on the other hand, the stabilisation and association agreement with montenegro itself contains a number of problematic provisions with which i cannot identify. among them, the first is the call and support for montenegro's integration into nato. as i have said on several occasions, i insist that the eu has no right to dictate to anyone to join an international military organisation, which nato is first and foremost. this approach of the european institutions appears in the context of the current events in ukraine as a pathological, rude, very unreasonable and denying the fundamental attribute of the sovereignty of the state to freely choose the method of its own defense. in view of these contradictions, i have therefore decided to abstain.
in writing. ‒ why did i vote against the adoption of the reports on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the importation into the union of agricultural products originating in turkey, when it is in fact a mere legal codification of the current situation? the reason is quite simple, i wanted to express my solidarity and solidarity with my colleagues in cyprus. as is well known, even after three decades of attempts at change, the island of cyprus is still divided into two parts, the republic of cyprus and the turkish republic of northern cyprus, which is occupied by turkish troops. in view of this situation and given that both codified versions also deal with the regulation of exports from the occupied territory of cyprus to the eu, i have decided to vote against these reports as an expression of my disagreement with the current political situation on this island, which is essentially an occupied eu member state.
in writing. ‒ i supported the agreement on the establishment of the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean. the european union joined the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean in 1998 to promote the sustainable development, conservation and rational management of living marine resources in the mediterranean and the black sea. the text set a clearer definition of the overall objective of the organisation in terms of biological, social, economic and environmental sustainability. the new agreement also includes core elements of the common fisheries policy, notably the fight against illegal fishing.
i, unlike my predecessor, supported this report. i believe that, even in view of the majority adopted, the vote was fully justified, because the report gives a credible picture of the situation in the section of the budget. i would like to mention two other points which i think are quite important, namely the question of support for smes, since they are also mentioned in the report. indeed, it must be stressed that they represent over 90% of all businesses operating in europe and have undoubtedly also been affected by the crisis. this role of enterprises should be linked to the operation of the structural and investment funds in the european union, as they are the main lever of investment expenditure, and this report should therefore be supported if it mentions this link. i'm glad i could be of support.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the guidelines for the eu budget for 2016, which present our priorities for future negotiations. the text clearly support job creation, but also companies and entrepreneurship, and this is essential, in my view, to create growth in the eu.

in writing. ‒ the recent luxleaks case demonstrated the need to tackle tax fraud in the eu more effectively. i voted in favour of the commission annual report for 2013 on the protection of the eu's financial interests and urge the member states to cooperate and coordinate with the commission on the matter. in 2013, 15 779 irregularities were reported to the commission, involving about 2.14 billion euros, and i find the growing trend alarming. many policy sectors are affected by fraud, and i call on the commission to establish uniform reporting principles in all member states so as to collect comparable and accurate data.

in writing. the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children constitute, in my view, one of the most serious forms of violation of fundamental rights as laid down in the 1989 united nations convention on the rights of the child and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. serious crimes such as the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography clearly require a comprehensive approach involving not only the prosecution of offenders but also, and above all, the protection and prevention of child victims themselves. international cooperation beyond the public sector is needed in this area and i therefore welcome the commission's initiative to set up a coalition for a better and safer internet for children, which also brings together 31 of the largest technology and media companies whose involvement could significantly strengthen our common fight against child abuse online.

i never forgot my encounters with boris nemtsov. his murder added a shakespearean touch to these memories. a man who loved life above all else and knew how to live it was murdered. he knew how to enjoy winning, but he also knew how to lose. he was a big, happy kid. he was also a man of his time and a participant in russia's destiny. i don't want to stir up emotions, which are usually more than healthy in this room. but i have to say that the negative reflex that some western politicians and journalists have in responding to all the information from russia is extremely inappropriate in this case. boris nemtsov was an opposition politician who liked russia. he was in opposition not because he wanted to unite the world against russia, but because he had a different view than the kremlin on the way to a good life in russia. his ideas have been marginalized for a variety of reasons. but that doesn't mean that they can't be a successful vision one day, that's political life. i'm deeply convinced that boris nemtsov would not approve if his death was used to spread anti-russian hysteria.

for the alde group. i am watching with great concern the impact of the german minimum wage law on european employers, and in particular on transport. each country is fully entitled to its own minimum wage law if it so chooses, but it is not possible for the application of such a law to be contrary to eu principles. this is clearly a violation of the fundamental principles of the free market and the free movement of persons and services. unfortunately, the german measure fits into the current trend of growing protectionism within the eu. the danger is that if germany defends the application of the law in this form, a chain reaction in other countries can be expected. in addition to the financial burden, we cannot ignore the huge increase in bureaucracy, which is contrary to the accepted european principle of smart regulation. can we really, in 21st century europe, require companies to fax documentation to cologne or to keep detailed records of their employees in german only? but i think that, in addition to the legal and technical aspects, the german minimum wage is a fundamental political problem for europe, it is a step backwards. instead of further unification, europe is building an invisible barrier between states. it denies the very purpose of the eu and the very purpose of our work. this afternoon i met with representatives of czech transport companies outside the parliament building, who are here, together with carriers from other countries, protesting against the german law. the protesters asked me what information i had, how the situation was developing. they're worried about survival, especially the small carriers. what could i tell them? nothing, commissioner, nothing. i was just... after weeks of questioning and waiting for the authorities to respond, we still have no solution. you know, the worst thing for any entrepreneur is uncertainty, and for me, uncertainty is unacceptable. this legal uncertainty has been going on for three months. so i ask you, commissioner, when will there really be a final, clear assessment? when will you have clear, unambiguous answers for our carriers and employers? please, will you publish the german answer you have had for more than three weeks? are you prepared to initiate a compliance procedure against germany? although the eu has made many progresses in building the single market, the new german minimum wage law goes against it. this is particularly remarkable in a time when we are trying to stimulate the economy by improving the investment environment, and we are building administrative barriers instead of breaking down barriers. i am personally glad that german workers finally have the right to a minimum wage. however, i am concerned that the german government has abused this to gain a competitive advantage and to seriously undermine the free movement of services in the internal market. full implementation of the german government's proposal would lead to the liquidation of the czech road hauliers. in addition to the significant financial burden, the implementation of the act also entails a significant administrative burden, which also does not contribute to the free movement of services in the internal market and, moreover, only applies to foreign carriers. the implementation of this legislation will lead to a deepening of the two-speed europe and is in fact a partial blockage of the labour market. we are calling for a clear statement from the european commission, which should consider whether it will be dragged along by the german government or whether it will really represent the interests of all member states and promote european law and the pillars on which the eu is built, including, for example, minimum social standards for workers across europe or even opening a debate on a pan-european minimum wage.
the debate on the application of the german minimum wage law is not limited to its compatibility with eu law, the legal uncertainties faced by carriers since 1 january this year and the complicated administrative burden. all of this needs to be resolved, and very soon, commissioner. in this respect, i too call for a rapid response to clarify the situation of the carriers in compliance with european law. the context of the debate is, of course, deeper and more long-term. some call it social dumping, others competitiveness based on lower costs, especially wages. in the eu's neighbouring countries, there are huge differences in the existence of the internal market and the free movement of services. the minimum wage in germany is four times higher than in the czech republic and is even twice as high as the czech average wage. the current situation in the transport sector has only shown the full extent of this problem. whatever the european commission decides, this contradiction will not disappear from europe.
i join my colleagues in strongly criticising the german authorities' decision on the minimum wage. if the system applied only to german carriers, it would of course be a german matter. unfortunately, this has a dramatic effect on businessmen in other countries, who are thus either forced to break domestic laws or face heavy sanctions fines from the german authorities. i'm very concerned that, based on the available figures, this could be a disaster for many, especially small businesses. the eu is founded on the fundamental principles of the free movement of people, goods and services between member states. but we see a clear breach of that principle here, and we don't want to see a series of counter-actions and a de facto classic trade war between eu member states. i therefore call on the german government to repeal and amend these measures immediately and on the commission to resolve the matter expeditiously.
the four freedoms that the internal market offers us - the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital - are, in my view, one of the greatest and, without doubt, most visible achievements of european integration. therefore, the national law of any of the member states may not restrict these freedoms. not only would we then face discrimination against other eu nationals, but we could also be the cause of their financial problems, or even their complete bankruptcy. the legislation currently being introduced by germany and seriously considered by other eu countries therefore runs counter to the four freedoms that the eu guarantees its citizens in certain sectors, namely transport. let us therefore seek solutions which do not jeopardise the functioning of the common market and thus do not harm the legitimate interests of businesses in other member states.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to continue and use my speaking time. today's debate on ecall, the seventh in all, follows the adoption by the council on 2 march this year of a position at first reading on a regulation on type-approval requirements for the deployment of an ecall in-vehicle system using the 112 emergency call line. the regulation is part of a package of initiatives to ensure the roll-out of the 112 ecall service across europe, free of charge to all consumers, regardless of vehicle type, purchase price or country of residence. as early as the beginning of last year, the european parliament and the member states adopted the decision to make ecall mandatory, which implements the pan-european infrastructure necessary for the proper functioning of the ecall emergency system in each member state from october 2017. the text presented here complements this decision and sets out the type-approval requirements for ecall in-vehicle devices. new types of passenger cars and light commercial vehicles are to be designed from 31 march 2018 to trigger the 112 emergency call automatically or manually in the event of a serious accident. the european parliament has long been one of the main supporters of the introduction of the ecall safety system. in the past, we have repeatedly pointed to the delays in voluntary deployment to date, which were caused by unavailability, high cost and inefficiencies on the way abroad. in july 2012, parliament called on the commission in a resolution to submit a proposal to introduce ecall as a public service. the requested proposal was presented by the commission in june 2013 and four parliamentary committees subsequently began working intensively on it. the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, the committee on transport and tourism, the committee on industry, research and energy and the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs supported the general line of the mandatory introduction of ecall and contributed with several specific provisions to reinforce or clarify the commission proposal. i would like to thank all the rapporteurs, shadow rapporteurs and colleagues for their cooperation and very valuable and helpful opinions. in february 2014, the european parliament adopted a position at first reading. this post-election position was the mandate for the final negotiations with the member states. the council, like the european parliament, made a number of changes to the original proposal. in the second half of last year, three trilogues and many other working meetings were held, resulting in an agreement between the two institutions in december. i would like to take this opportunity to thank the italian and latvian presidencies for their intensive and very constructive cooperation. the role of the italian presidency in particular has been crucial. i would also like to thank the commission, which also made a significant contribution to the compromise reached. the european parliament succeeded in pushing through the vast majority of the amendments during the negotiations, including an explicit reference to the 112 emergency call line, compatibility with satellite navigation systems, reporting and review, and an incentive for the commission to further intensify its work on value-added services that could bring additional benefits to consumers and enhance the competitiveness of european industry. a big thank you goes to all the members of the negotiating team, the secretariat and the services of the european parliament for their excellent assistance. the resulting text also fully guarantees the right to privacy and data protection, which has been paramount for the european parliament from the outset. the in-depth work of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs has contributed to the detailed clarification of the rules on privacy and data protection. a vehicle equipped with an ecall system shall not be traceable in normal operating conditions and shall not be subject to any permanent recording of its position. the system shall remain inactive until the distress call is triggered. the data set sent by ecall to the emergency services will only contain the minimum information required for the proper handling of emergency calls and will only be provided to the emergency services. in addition, the data stored in the system's internal memory shall be automatically and permanently erased. contrary to the european parliament's initial call, the date of entry into force of the regulation has been postponed. the launch of the system requires close cooperation between several actors involved and member states have asked for more time to put the necessary infrastructure in place. i think it is reasonable to meet this requirement so that the system is 100% operational at launch and can be fully trusted by european citizens. in view of the above, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to ask you to vote tomorrow in favour of the text without further amendments. the agreement, which was supported by the member states, sets out the priorities of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection and the opinions of the associated committees, is consistent with the mandate given to me as rapporteur by the vote of the european parliament's plenary in first reading and is in line with previous requests by the european parliament. thank you for your attention, and i look forward to the next debate.
the rapporteur. let me close this debate by thanking all my colleagues for their contributions and for the support they have shown throughout the legislative process, which, as some of you have mentioned, was not short. as i have already said, i was aware from the outset of the criticisms of the system and i am therefore convinced that the european parliament, together with the member states, has succeeded in taking these criticisms into account in the final text. ladies and gentlemen, i conclude by saying that i am convinced that the introduction of ecall across the european union will make a significant contribution to improving the safety of european road users, although i agree that i am certainly not the only one. the european parliament has repeatedly identified reducing the number of deaths and injuries on european roads as one of its priorities, and i believe that tomorrow's vote will contribute to our common objective.
in writing.– the ecall emergency system is clearly a step forward in increasing the safety of citizens. i would like to thank my colleague olga sehnalová for her work. i do, however, believe that citizens should have the choice on whether to participate in the ecall system or not. i agree that measures that directly save lives in an accident should be mandatory. a seat belt, for example, can mean the difference between life and death. the ecall system could help in the aftermath of an accident, but will not prevent it. the ecall would instead increase the chances of paramedics coming to the scene earlier, in the event that no one in the car is able to make a phone call or there is no other witness around to call emergency services. although the ecall system could potentially save lives, it is not a vital component and therefore each citizen must be given the right to decide if the benefits outweigh the cost, which is the sharing of their information.

mr president, i would like to explain why i did not vote for the motion to reject this directive. the directive only concerns one detail, plastic bags, which have an impact on the environment. igelite bags having a wall thickness of 15 to 50 microns. so these are lightweight plastic bags. the directive does not impose any obligation on member states, but gives them the choice of which tool to use to reduce consumption, whether it be charging or limiting the number of plastic carrier bags. the labelling of compostable materials and the push for research to recycle these plastic bags are also important measures. i expect the european union to tackle problems that the member states cannot, and environmental protection is one of those issues. that is why i supported this directive.
in writing. on 28 april 2015, the european parliament voted on a directive amending directive 94/62/ec as regards the restriction of the consumption of lightweight plastic shopping bags. i voted against the rejection of the november 2014 text, which was the result of long interinstitutional negotiations between the council, the european parliament and the commission, because i consider it to be of high quality and helpful to environmental protection. if we reject the new amendment, it will only worsen the overall situation. billions of plastic bags end up as waste each year, polluting the oceans and seas, where they gradually break down into smaller and smaller particles and disrupt food chains. today, we're talking about enough plastic in the oceans to create a whole new continent. the text of the directive aims to halve the consumption of these bags within three years and to reduce it by a fifth within ten years. one of the biggest advantages of the new regulation, i see, is that it does not necessarily require artificial intervention to increase the price of these plastic bags. member states will have a choice between two options: either to take measures to ensure that the average annual consumption of lightweight plastic carrier bags per citizen does not exceed 90 pieces by 2019 and 40 pieces by 2025, or to ensure that by 2018 these bags are not provided free of charge by traders.
in writing. ‒ i do not agree with the european union telling consumers what to carry with them when they shop. i have therefore proposed the rejection of this directive, which would end its legislative process.
in writing. ‒ the proposal newly includes an obligation for member states to achieve a sustainable reduction in the consumption of lightweight plastic shopping bags. i am glad that the european parliament has gone further than the commission's original proposal in this respect. i am convinced that the proposal will not have the effect of placing excessive demands on eu citizens, but will instead provide them with an adequate incentive to protect natural resources. eu member states must now ensure that the annual consumption of lightweight plastic shopping bags does not exceed 90 pieces/person by 2019 (and 40 bags/person by the end of 2025). i also consider it essential to call on the commission to come forward as soon as possible with proposals for the labelling of biodegradable and compostable plastic bags. the lack of a uniform label so far means that products with different levels of biodegradability are labelled as biodegradable or compostable (some products, even in the process of decomposition, can cause more harm to nature than good, in particular the so-called oxo-biological bags), thus depriving the term biodegradable of its meaning and not guaranteeing to the consumer that it really does good for the protection of nature. the regulation adopted by parliament does not cover so-called very lightweight plastic bags (such as plastic bags used for buying fruit) which are necessary for hygiene reasons and to prevent waste. but in the future, we're going to have to find meaningful and realistic solutions to deal with this problem as well.
in writing. i see the obligation of member states to achieve a lasting reduction in the consumption of lightweight plastic shopping bags as an obligation for each of us to work towards reducing the environmental burden and to try to prevent further unnecessary pollution. for the first time in 40 years of european waste legislation, we will have binding measures at eu level to reduce waste generation. it's about time.

the reporter. madam president, mr president of the court of auditors, before approving the report on discharge to the european development fund which i am presenting, is it perhaps the right moment to reflect on what we actually expect from this development fund? its importance and significance were unintentionally reminded of quite recently by another tragedy off the coast of the italian island of lampedusa. in the heated debate on migration, asylum and development policy in the european union, it may not have been clear enough that the european development fund is the instrument that should help to prevent a repeat of this. yes, we expect the fund to use its limited resources to overcome the causes of extreme poverty in countries with unsustainable economic development and failing public institutions, in countries torn by political and social crises. the european development fund cannot eliminate this unhappy situation altogether, but it can try to prevent some undesirable phenomena, such as the increasing and life-threatening emigration of desperate people to european countries, by systematic aid. as regards the discharge for the european development fund, i consider it to be significant for at least three reasons: the first is to evaluate its functioning to date. let's learn from our mistakes and be inspired by what we've done well. the second reason is the need to set the priorities of the fund in the light of the changing needs of the developing world in relation to the european union. finally, the third reason is our recommendations for the continued operation of the fund in the longer term. of course, on the basis of efficiency and transparency. we have a lot of experience and insight into how the support system has worked so far. in my opinion, it's time to abandon some of the stereotypes we've been used to. for example, in terms of risks in the beneficiary countries. the risk was simply taken for granted and this was matched by a relatively high error rate in the projects considered, which, moreover, did not produce the desired effect. similarly, the monitoring and control system has not always been able to address the deficiencies identified. even with the overall high contribution of the aid, there were certainly some cases where the situation was not optimal. i therefore consider it necessary to take the following steps: let us assess the strategic priorities of the european development fund that we have jointly set and focus on the really important areas where we will implement further projects to support entrepreneurship, infrastructure development or to address urgent social issues. this requires a significant reduction in error rates, a focus on content priorities and the choice of the financial instrument and project management that best achieve the objectives. in implementing aid, we must be aware of the differences in conditions between developing and european countries. we cannot rely exclusively on local intermediaries, but the solution is not to adopt european practices entirely either. we should really be sensitive and objective in balancing the economic and political motives and incentives for aid, because we have a duty to monitor the effectiveness of financial instruments as well. the european development fund should be seen as a meaningful return on investment, not just a gift from a 'rich european uncle'. our report agrees that we need precise, transparent and strategic priorities that respond to real and current needs. the use of modern financial instruments can lead to enhanced efficiency and transparency. we recommend that a functional management, monitoring and control system be adopted. finally, we recommend that the european development fund should become an integral part of the budget of the european union. then we can use the funds immediately and quickly to help where it is urgently needed. i thank all the shadow rapporteurs for their exemplary and creative cooperation, and i thank the commission and the european court of auditors for their excellent cooperation.

author. mr president, allow me to briefly present a question on behalf of the committee on legal affairs concerning the marrakesh treaty on the facilitation of access to published works for blind and visually impaired persons or persons with other reading disabilities. this international agreement was negotiated within the world intellectual property organization and adopted in june 2013. the european union signed the treaty on 30 april 2014 but has not yet ratified it. the marrakesh treaty introduces a set of rules which allow for the existence of restrictions or exceptions to copyright at national level for the benefit of persons who are blind or visually impaired, and which also ensure the cross-border exchange of accessible format copies of published works for which copyright exceptions have been granted. the contract allows various organisations providing services to the blind and visually impaired to make copies of works accessible to such persons in accessible formats, to lend such copies or to make them available by electronic means on a non-profit basis. the treaty thus brings significant improvements to the situation of blind and visually impaired citizens, who are eagerly awaiting its entry into force. the question at this stage is therefore, first of all, when can we expect the council to take a decision on ratifying the marrakesh treaty and why has this not yet happened? if there are legal doubts on the part of some member states as to whether all the provisions of the treaty fall within the exclusive competence of the european union, we would welcome an active approach by the presidency to ensure that these uncertainties are quickly clarified and lead, as a result, to the ratification of the treaty and its entry into force. the european parliament is certainly ready to help in this matter. i believe that, particularly in the case of an international treaty which has a clear humanitarian and social dimension, because it significantly improves the situation of disabled eu citizens, a satisfactory solution should be actively pursued. i personally think that ratification should not wait for the outcome of the debate on the reform of the eu copyright system, which has not yet begun and will probably take some time. i hope, therefore, that the doubts will soon be removed and that the marrakesh treaty can be ratified.

mr president, i listened with interest to what the vice-president of the commission said and i would like to say that i have always supported low and simple taxes. the example of e-books that we're debating here today clearly shows that if the tax system is complex and has a whole bunch of exceptions, then there are interpretation problems that come with it. when justice and the court remove these problems, absurd situations often occur. an example is the case of the relationship between printed books and electronic books, where different media, different information carriers are taxed differently. i would like you, mr vice-president of the commission, to see this case as an example of how exemptions and a complex tax system do not work. if you're talking about the commission preparing a definitive vat system, you should learn from this case. because the problem, in my opinion, is not the decision of the court of justice of the european union. i read the verdict, and the verdict is correct in my opinion. the problem is the directive, which is vague and unclear about the exceptions. so we should talk about if exceptions are to be defined, and if they are, then to the smallest extent possible. i'm asking you to fix the problem, and like my colleagues, i'm calling for support for the digital market. i am convinced that the absurd situation where only a different medium brings in double vat on books, printed books on the one hand and electronic books on the other, should have been eliminated long ago. so please remove it in the interest of developing a digital single market.
mr president, one of the key priorities of the commission is the digital single market strategy. the vat on e—books, i think, is an excellent example where we can show that we are committed to this agenda and that we are able to deliver without delay to our citizens. i do not see any reason why i should pay twice as much in taxes on e—books than on books in their physical form. the rise in the price of e—books was never intended. it was an unforeseen consequence, an error, and now is the time to fix it. we all speak about the urgency of this topic. i am looking forward to your vat proposal in 2016, but meanwhile here is one suggestion: why do you not propose an urgent single sentence amendment to the 2006 vat directive allowing digital books, newspapers and magazines the same reductions already allowed for their physical counterparts? it would only require three words to be added to the annex to fix it. the words are: ‘physical or digital’. let us solve this in the simplest and quickest way possible. let us make this an example where europe sees an error and fixes it; where europe embraces our digital future.

in writing. ‒ following the recent terrorist attacks in paris, brussels and copenhagen, it was crucial that the european union took decisive action against anti money laundering and terrorist financing. i believe this new directive is part of the answer. it will facilitate the work of financial intelligence units from different member states to identify and follow suspicious transfers of money, facilitate the exchange of information and ensure full traceability of funds transfers within, to, and from the eu. moreover, these new rules reflect the legitimate public demand for increased transparency in this field. it will for the first time oblige eu member states to keep central registers of information on the ultimate ‘beneficial’ owners of corporate and other legal entities, as well as trusts, a strong demand from the european parliament. there is still room for improvement when it comes to the accessibility of the public register, but the directive leaves the door open to those member states which are ready, to move forward. i strongly encourage them to use the available flexibility to provide unrestricted public registers with access to beneficial ownership information for companies and trusts.
in writing. i welcome the final form of the directive, which is a compromise between the ep and the council, retaining most of the elements put forward by the ep at first reading. all companies registered in eu member states will thus be required to provide information on their owners, down to the level of natural persons. this information will be collected in a mandatory central register of beneficial owners, which will be publicly accessible. i consider this an important step towards greater transparency of financial flows and a reduction in tax evasion. i believe that this will also be an impulse for the czech government to adopt legislation leading to the disclosure of the owners of all public limited companies.
