in writing. i supported the compromise agreement between the ep and the council, which will provide financial intelligence units and law enforcement agencies with more information to enable better traceability of payments. the resulting format also ensures that the eu legal framework will continue to be fully in line with international standards. it is useful to provide for an obligation for payment service providers to transmit information not only on the payer but also on the payee throughout the payment chain for the purposes of preventing, investigating and detecting money laundering and terrorist financing. the uniform implementation of the new rules throughout the european union should ensure that there is no distinction between cases involving national payments within a member state and cross-border payments between member states. at the same time, all such mechanisms needed today must be fully clear and transparent in terms of how information is used and defended against misuse.
in writing. on 19 may 2015, at the plenary session in strasbourg, we discussed an important revision of the regulation governing insolvency proceedings. i must say at the outset that i welcome the commission's efforts to modernise insolvency law, not only in the light of the scandalous abuse of this right in the czech republic. i believe that the proposal presented can lead to a reduction in the notorious 'insolvency tourism' and to the modernisation of the resolution of so-called crossborder insolvency cases which is now necessary. however, despite my support for this document, i still see a number of shortcomings. in my view, the planned revision should in particular increase the protection of those most at risk, namely employees affected by the possible bankruptcy of their company. in the czech republic, company insolvencies are now commonplace, with the number of proceedings opened having increased almost sevenfold in the last six years alone. we need not only a broader discussion on how to protect companies from bankruptcy, but also, especially in the context of the situation in the czech republic, a discussion on how to prevent their frequent and unregulated abuse in the context of competition between entrepreneurs. one of the realistic ways i would see, for example, is to deprive creditors of the possibility to file so-called creditor insolvency applications. it is still absolutely unacceptable that almost one in ten companies in the czech republic have been exposed to similar practices, according to the available data.
in writing. i consider the revision of the insolvency regulation to be an important step towards modernising insolvency law. i believe that there is a particular need to increase the protection of employees, who are most affected by the eventual bankruptcy of their employer. unfortunately, the risk of companies going bankrupt is high today, for example in the czech republic the number of insolvency applications has increased from 5 300 to more than 35 000 cases per year in the last 6 years. so we need a broader discussion about how to protect companies from going bankrupt. another problem i see is so-called insolvency tourism and the filing of harassing insolvency petitions in order to eliminate competition. this means that companies that do not actually owe anyone anything can be put on the insolvency register. according to statistics, one in ten companies in the czech republic has encountered such a harassing insolvency proposal. i need not add that such a situation would seriously damage the company concerned. i support the effort to modernise insolvency law, but because i am convinced that this document does not guarantee adequate protection for employees, i abstained from voting.
in writing. i supported the proposal for new rules on insolvency proceedings because i believe it is a good example of useful eu legislation that helps to deal with situations with an increasingly cross-border element. in particular, i welcome the fact that the new rules also aim to eliminate forum shopping and introduce an online database of ongoing crossborder proceedings.
in writing. ‒ we must have stronger mechanisms that support the respect of human rights and business transparency in the areas where minerals are extracted. to truly change things on the ground, we need a system that will work in practice. this is why i supported a mandatory due diligence system for all smelters, refiners and importers of minerals, because it can realistically be implemented and hit hard where it matters. it is, however, simply not feasible to include a mandatory approach to all downstream companies in the supply chain. these companies would struggle to obtain the information from all their different suppliers, and it will be the smes that will mostly be penalised. if this mandatory system for all actually could work in practice, then it would have my full support. but as we have seen with the us example of dodd-frank, going further in legislation does not always mean we get the desired results.
in writing. the great lakes region of africa is a place of frequent conflict, with minerals and metals playing a vital role. a cursory glance at the history of the countries in the region that lie (i.e. burundi, the democratic republic of congo, kenya, rwanda, tanzania and uganda) shows that this soil is soaked in the blood of civil wars and genocide. the european parliament has decided to help at least a little to alleviate the difficult situation in which the region finds itself. the left-wing forces in the european parliament have made it clear that they want a certification system to be introduced to make it clear that minerals and metals do not come from conflict zones and are therefore not, for example, so-called blood diamonds. today, consumers are often indirectly linked to conflicts that have serious implications for the peaceful development of the region. human rights abuses in the mining industry are common, which may include child labour, sexual violence, enforced disappearances, forced displacement and the destruction of ritually or culturally significant sites. the great lakes region should be a place of democracy and education, not of inhuman practices to increase profits, which then end up in the pockets of self-styled leaders or arms and drug dealers. anything that helps stop this, i'm happy to support, as is this motion.
in writing. ‒ it is a naive attempt to prevent human rights abuses in the extraction of precious minerals. but making regulations doesn't help people. at best, it will drive smaller firms out of the market and empower large corporations. i have nothing against voluntary certification of companies. but there is no need for an eu directive.
in writing. ‒ i am glad at the result achieved by parliament on the s&d proposals of establishing a eu system for supply chain due diligence self-certification of responsible importers of metal in conflict areas. regarding continuing conflicts and suffering around the world, it is important that we ensure a disconnection between conflict financing and mineral extraction to promote economic transparency and, most importantly, human rights. it is therefore equally crucial when it comes to making solid changes of situations in high-risk areas to introduce a mandatory scheme of due diligence for the entire supply chain to guarantee the traceability of not only imported metals, but also of all natural resources from such areas. meanwhile, i am also convinced that special attention and flexibility should be designated to the smes along with the requirement of a mandatory self—declaration as a responsible importer. with the voice of parliament demanding an exclusion of conflict metals in the eu market, i look forward to a final resolution, in accord with the commission and council, being adopted to put the approach of achieving human rights into practice.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the text calling for a european certification system for smelters and refiners of tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold, in order to stop the exploitative and deadly trade in conflict minerals. this eu legislation should serve as a model to create a positive dynamic in other parts of the world to put an end to the exploitation of minerals that are funding conflicts.
in writing. the dangerous substances restriction directive, adopted in 2011, temporarily excluded the use of cadmium in leds for lighting and display components until july 2014. however, in january this year, the commission surprisingly proposed, by means of a delegated act, a further extension of the use of cadmium in televisions until june 2018. in my view, the commission was therefore essentially seeking to reintroduce cadmium on the eu market, as some producers have already fully started to remove cadmium from their products, following the expiry of the original exemption in july 2014. the commission's reasoning is that, according to it, cadmium-free quantum dots are not technically available at present. however, in my view, this is only a trade conflict between two groups of producers, where one has already developed and successfully introduced the necessary technology, the other has not yet and is asking the commission for more time. in this light, and on the basis of the analysis provided by the legal service of the european parliament, which assured us that the rejection of this delegated act does not mean the prohibition of cadmium in quantum dots, as the original exemption remains in force, i have decided to support a resolution that will not allow the use of cadmium in diodes to be extended. and that is also because the resolution i supported calls for a re-examination of the extension of the derogation.
in writing. ‒ i voted against because i believe that the commission's proposal in this case, exceptionally, means less regulation and unnecessary prohibitions.
in writing. i voted against the motion for a resolution by which the ep objects to the commission delegated directive amending, for the purposes of adapting to technical progress, annex iii to directive 2011/65/eu of the european parliament and of the council as regards the exemption for the use of cadmium in lighting and display systems. i believe that the exemption for the use of cadmium, which covers a wider range of lighting and visual technologies (typically mobile phones, monitors, televisions, tablets), is justified today. while i am generally in favour of reducing health risks, cadmium-free technologies do not seem to be ready to meet the demands of the market today, for example, due to low energy efficiency and short life problems. to my knowledge, there is not enough technology on the global market without the presence of cadmium. i am afraid that the repeal of the exemption will mean the destruction of investments made by the lighting industry in particular to improve energy efficiency, and therefore i think it may be premature.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution, in which the european parliament objects to the european commission's directive granting an exemption for the use of cadmium in lighting and display systems. the industry uses quantum dot technology based on cadmium, a toxic element. this exemption may be granted where technical progress does not allow the dangerous element to be replaced by another or where it would be an economically unsustainable production method. but since these cadmium-free technologies are already on the market and are comparable in performance to, or even superior to, cadmium-based technologies, i do not think it is necessary or desirable to allow an exemption and thus to extend the production of cadmium-based technologies that are demonstrably harmful to the human body. that's why i voted against the waiver.
in writing. ‒ i decided to support the objection to the delegated act on exemption for cadmium in illumination and display lighting applications. cadmium is a highly toxic metal the use of which is restricted to cases where there is no substitute: illuminations and display lightings fall under this exception. the exemption came to an end in 2014 and the commission is asking, through a delegated act, to renew it. i am opposing it because the exception is based on outdated information and may no longer be justified. opposing the delegated act does not mean immediate banning of cadmium as the exemption will remain until a decision is taken. what i want is to send the decision back to the commission for a thorough technical assessment, in line with an objective of better regulation.
in writing. ‒ i voted against because i believe that this commission proposal is exceptionally less regulatory and more pro-business. i'm not in favor of putting in more ethanol-related red tape.

in writing. ‒ i voted against the resolution on maternity leave. parliament has decided to vote for a resolution which would prescribe 20 paid weeks of maternity leave (of which only 6 fully paid) and a call for a different proposal for fathers allowing them to take paid leave for 10 days. it is hard for me to agree that such proposals would add value, stand for more equal rights for mothers and fathers and would progress gender equality, in particular in relation to working mothers. first, my question is why do we need to treat parents of one kid in two different pieces of legislation? second, i find the standards set by both proposals very low and discriminatory towards parents of different sexes. in addition, they would create clear inequality between parents of the same sex. the commission should have the right to withdraw this outdated proposal and revise the 2010 parental leave directive to allow both parents, irrespective of their sex, to take, on equal terms, paid leave and to decide who stays at home. if not, it should be left to the member states to continue their own policies which, in most cases, are much more generous, dynamic and flexible.

madam president, unlike my predecessors, i believe that the common foreign and security policy should be as much common to all the countries of the european union as possible, and should be so common that it should be a common single policy. i think that in this collective strength there is then a far greater strength of all the nations that are united within the european union. unlike my colleagues, i believe that this represents a huge opportunity to promote europe's voice throughout an increasingly globalised world. i would like to open with one more point, which concerns defence policy, namely its duplication with nato forces. i have long held the position that nato should not be duplicated by the european union in defence policy. however, the events in ukraine and the inability of the european union to directly intervene in this conflict with a reasonable solution, is, i think, a question for defence policy.
in writing. i voted against this resolution, which also contains paragraph 38, in which the parliament says that it is surprised that there are still no tax incentive mechanisms at eu level for cooperation and pooling of resources [in defence and security policy] and is convinced that such exemptions [from vat] must be applied systematically and calls for the creation of any other incentives that could stimulate cooperation between european stakeholders. the commission is therefore calling for more action on the common defence and security policy, possibly with a view to building a european army, as high representative mogherini has said. i do not agree that the european union should have its own security and defence policy, let alone its own army. as a defence alliance in europe, nato serves the member states well and it is neither necessary nor desirable to duplicate or compete with the european defence alliance.
‒ the security situation in the eu, especially in its eastern and southern neighbourhood, is becoming increasingly volatile and variable, due to a large number of long-standing and emerging security challenges. the conflict in eastern ukraine, the conflicts in syria and iraq, the rise of the terrorist organisation daesh, the libyan crisis and the terrorist threat in africa (in particular in the sahel, libya and the horn of africa) all pose an immediate threat to the security of the union. i consider it necessary for the union and the member states to take greater responsibility for their own security and defence and to be able to respond effectively in an emergency. it is therefore entirely appropriate to make a joint and coordinated effort within the cfsp/cfsp framework to develop a new common european security strategy that defines the geostrategic scenarios, threats and global challenges that have emerged and more precisely outlines the actions that the eu can take in response to them. particular attention needs to be paid to the integration of cyber defence into member states' national security strategies, as cyber attacks have increased in recent years and this trend is expected to continue. i am confident that the european council will agree at its june meeting on further concrete steps leading to more effective and deeper pan-european coordination of security policy, including on the question of funding.
in writing. ‒ i am of course in favour of security and defence policy and believe that we need to work together and invest appropriately in defence policy. this must not happen in the context of parallel structures leading to the weakening of nato, which is the basis of the common defence policy. we should generally avoid any defence activities outside nato, and that is why i could not support this report as it stands.
in writing. i voted against this resolution, which also contains paragraph 28, in which parliament is concerned that there are still no mechanisms at european level to provide tax incentives for cooperation and sharing [within the framework of the common defence and security policy] and recognises that these exemptions [from vat] must be systematic and extended to infrastructure and specific capacity-building programmes and calls for the development of any other incentive mechanisms that could promote cooperation in capacity between europeans. the commission is therefore calling for more action on the common defence and security policy, possibly with a view to building a european army, as high representative mogherini has said. i do not agree that the european union should have its own security and defence policy, let alone its own army. as a defence alliance in europe, nato serves the member states well and it is neither necessary nor desirable to duplicate or compete with the european defence alliance.
‒ i voted against this resolution, which also contains paragraph 13, in which parliament calls for cooperation and association and joint use of initiatives to be considered as a priority area, calls on the european commission to propose [...] how tax incentives could contribute to achieving these objectives, considers that the projects of the european defence agency should be exempt from vat and expects that it will include measures to promote cooperative purchases of defence equipment and the provision of appropriate support. the commission is therefore calling for more action on the common defence and security policy, possibly with a view to building a european army, as high representative mogherini has said. i do not agree that the european union should have its own security and defence policy, let alone its own army. as a defence alliance in europe, nato serves the member states well and it is neither necessary nor desirable to duplicate or compete with the european defence alliance.
in writing. i have supported the report by mrs gomes and i also thank you for including my comments which respond to the recent negative experience with the storage of military equipment in the czech republic. last year, two citizens were killed in uncontrolled explosions at the ammunition storage facility in vrbetica, hundreds of people were temporarily forced to stay away from their homes, and the damage caused by the actions of a private entity came to tens of millions of crowns from the public budget. this tragedy has confirmed the importance of regular checks on all defence and security equipment by the responsible authorities, including the maintenance of proper records. i also welcome the fact that the report stresses that the procurement of defence and security equipment must take into account the need to ensure the highest level of protection and safety for the civilian population. i hope that the member states will join the european parliament in this challenge.

on behalf of the alde group.– madam president, the alde group fully supports free and open media, and that is why we must do more to protect them from cyber-attacks. cyber-attacks on the media come in two forms: one on the information shared with the public, and the other on the actual sources of journalism information. both endanger our trust in a free media. on the public side, in only a few years what was a game for hackers, vandalising media websites and twitter accounts has been transformed into tools of misinformation and panic-mongering. false information placed on twitter has already led to panics on the stock market. cyber-attacks on the media have been used in warfare to cut off information to citizens: such attacks go all the way back to the war in georgia. and now hacked broadcasts are being used as propaganda for terrorist organisations. on the other side, journalists’ email accounts and networks are being hacked. the identities of whistle-blowers and anonymous sources are becoming known. these cyber-attacks come not only from criminal organisations but also from the misuse of government resources. without better protection, this will have a chilling effect on investigative journalism. as cases like ‘luxleaks’ have shown, we need strong investigative journalism in order to keep our businesses and governments straight. as our citizens move online for all their information and the rate of information exchange keeps increasing, we must find ways to help our media organisations adapt to the new threats facing them. freedom of the press today must mean more than the right to print what you believe: it must also mean that your readers’ trust will not be abused by hackers or criminals.
commissioner, first of all, i would like to say on behalf of our ppe group that i absolutely condemn the cyber attacks on the media that have taken place in recent months. whether it was the attack on french tv5 or the belgian newspaper le soir. cybercrime is a threat to every country, every business and every citizen because its consequences are unpredictable. it is increasingly clear that the eu is not sufficiently protected against such attacks and is not prepared to defend itself. these attacks could come at any time, anywhere. after all, there is no way that we cannot provide a high level of security for our most important networks, like transportation, energy, and healthcare, where there is an enormous amount of private data and data from state-owned enterprises. the main thing we are lacking at the moment is the interconnectedness and close cooperation at eu member state level. yes, commissioner, in 2013 we established a cyber-attack centre at europol in the hague. i had the opportunity to visit him personally. but we have to say that we have not given him enough financial coverage, that is, he does not have enough funds, and we should change this situation as soon as possible. so i would like to call on the member states in particular to help, to work together on common infrastructure, and on the european commission to try to prepare networks and authorities for attacks from outside.

in writing. this year marks the 20th anniversary of the adoption of the beijing platform for action, which commits states to adhere to the set targets for achieving gender equality. however, when assessing the progress made since its adoption, it is clear that equality between women and men is only slowly being achieved. the european union should therefore adopt a strategy for the next five years. the report by mrs noichlov, whom i supported by voting in favour of it, also calls for this. it is unacceptable that the gender pay gap in some eu countries still reaches 30% and that women are therefore more at risk of poverty. this is also due to the higher proportion of women in part-time and precarious work, which results in lower pensions. the reconciliation of family and work life also remains problematic.
in writing. i voted against the report on the eu strategy for equality between women and men for the period after 2015 today, as unfortunately the resulting text does not take into account the amendments of the ppe, which were guided by the desire not to link the issue of equality between women and men with issues of reproductive health or the rights of persons with different sexual orientations, moreover in a way that violates the principle of subsidiarity, which should be applied to these issues.
in writing. ‒ it is unfortunate that in the 21st century women are not only facing unequal treatment at work, including lower remuneration, as well as other forms of discrimination in certain segments of society, but are regrettably facing harassment and violence. i see the report as a way of strengthening focus on this problem and attempt of introducing appropriate measures. that is why i have decided to vote in favour of the report as such, while i have voted against a number of amendments (on gender quota or the inclusion of a maternity leave). some amendments do not respect the principle of subsidiarity, some focus on measures which would increase significantly the administrative burden but would hardly achieve a proportionate result, regarding some one cannot have but serious doubts as concerns their relevance. i also found unacceptable those amendments which would affect public procurement rules or had the ambition to introduce legal acts of criminal nature. as this is an own-initiative report and thus a declaratory political document, i voted in favour of the report regardless of some of the amendments. i subscribe to the political message but remain firm in my opposition to gender quotas and references to maternity leave at european level.
in writing. ‒ the issue of gender equality needs to be addressed, but this report goes beyond the eu treaties and thus violates the principle of subsidiarity. by approving this text, the european parliament gives the european commission its consent to act in areas in which it has no competence and in which it should not intervene. i could therefore not support the report as it was drafted.
in writing. in my view, the main objective of european policy in this area should be to develop strong and firm strategies that would eventually lead to the elimination of the various forms of discrimination against women and men. gender equality in employment, social policy and the economy must be seen as a strategic and universal goal for the future, and not just beyond 2015.
in writing. i also supported the report on the strategy for the protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights in third countries because it is a fitting complement to the report on the road to a renewed consensus on the enforcement of intellectual property rights: an eu action plan, for which i was the rapporteur. both reports acknowledge the irreplaceable role of intellectual property rights in the pursuit and development of the modern 21st century economy. both reports highlight the need for greater coherence between the rules governing intellectual property rights inside and outside the european union. both reports also highlight the need for up-to-date, objective information and for achieving the broadest possible consensus on the role of intellectual property rights and the tools needed to enforce them effectively.
in writing. ‒ in my opinion, it is necessary to be aware of the dangers involved in buying goods that infringe intellectual property rights. i would suggest that consumers should be made more aware of the risks that people in third countries have to take. due to digitisation, intellectual property infringements have multiplied many times over, mainly due to the increasing sales on the internet. the adoption of a more effective tool for controlling the online sales of physical products would be clearly helpful. in view of these facts, i fully support the eu action plan on intellectual property rights in third countries.
in writing. on 9 june 2015, i supported the report of my czech colleague, mr pavlo svoboda, entitled 'intellectual property rights: an eu action plan', because i believe that the protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights contribute to generalised growth and much-needed job creation across the union. the document addresses the economic, social and even health impacts of infringement of intellectual property rights and their protection, also in the context of the eu charter of fundamental rights. in my view, if we want to further develop and ensure the proper functioning of the eu single market, which the czech republic has always consistently supported, we have no choice but to prevent the tax and economic losses that infringement of intellectual property rights represents for eu member states. the biggest problem with infringement i see is in the case of young people who continue to live in the spirit of the age of the internet's wild growth over the past two decades, when there was almost no protection of intellectual property rights on the internet, and they mistakenly believe that everything on the internet is free. it is therefore not only in this group that there is a need to intensively develop knowledge of the social and cultural significance of the protection of intellectual property rights.
‒ the development of new technologies, especially digital ones, also brings with it the requirement for adequate protection of intellectual property rights. i believe that infringements of intellectual property rights cause economic damage to european businesses and economic and tax losses to states. it is clear that people lack adequate knowledge of the social and cultural significance of intellectual property rights protection and of the activities considered to infringe them, and that young europeans in particular are not sufficiently aware of the possible impacts of intellectual property rights infringement i believe that the enforcement of intellectual property rights not only contributes to job creation and growth across the union, but is also a prerequisite for the proper functioning of the single market, in particular in view of factors such as the share of eu gdp, employment and the scale of industries that benefit from and use intellectual property rights. protection through intellectual property rights also plays an important role in stimulating innovation, creativity, competitiveness and cultural diversity. to better protect and inform consumers, we need an action plan to enforce intellectual property rights at eu level, which is why i supported the report.
in writing. i supported the report on the action plan on rights because i believe that the eu should make a significant effort in this area. infringements of intellectual property rights, including the widespread practice of counterfeiting, impede economic growth, job creation and innovation and cause serious economic and tax losses. and it's discouraging economic activity in this area. the trend of a significant proportion of europeans to consider infringement of intellectual property rights to be acceptable is a worrying finding. it is therefore necessary to increase users' awareness and knowledge of intellectual property rights, in particular in the digital environment, which brings new temptations and opportunities for infringement.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on an eu action plan on intellectual property rights (ipr). the eu needs innovation and creativity to stay competitive and intellectual property is a key driver for our growth. we have to fight counterfeiting to enhance the eu’s industrial competitiveness globally. that is why i am in favour of the creation of an eu action plan to ensure the effective, evidence-based enforcement of ipr, which play a key role in stimulating innovation, creativity, competitiveness, growth and cultural diversity. moreover, in respect to the better regulation objectives, i fully agree that measures taken to enforce ipr should be based on precise, reliable data.
for the group gue/ngl. let me thank both rapporteurs for what i think is a great report and the commissioner for being with us today. the kyoto protocol was signed back in 1997, but it was never ratified by the biggest polluters, like the us or china. i would like to remind all my colleagues here that after the united states finally refused to ratify the protocol, its fate was in the hands of russia. yes, it was precisely what some of you call the terrible russia, which has been portrayed here many times over the last year as the very bottom of hell that the fight against climate change has made possible. if russia could sign this agreement, i see no compelling argument why the protocol and its amendments could not be signed by our most important trading partner, the united states of america. in 2012, in doha, the parties to the protocol adopted an amendment to the protocol, introducing a second commitment period from 2013 to 2020. yes, the eu and iceland's continued participation in the second review period of the protocol helps our fight against climate change, but this step is completely negligible if we cannot ensure the participation of the biggest polluters, such as china, india or the united states, whose share of emissions was only about 36% in the original protocol. let's say it loud and clear: the current emissions from the eu and iceland are not a problem, they are a gesture from the eu. without the biggest polluters, the eu cannot do anything alone, which is why we must urge these countries to join us during the upcoming paris climate change conference.
draftswoman of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety. the european energy security strategy contains some really good points which can improve the quality of the environment in our view, so as to achieve a balance between ecological and socio-economic factors. first and foremost, it is about energy efficiency. the full exploitation of its potential and the development of smart infrastructure would stimulate growth and create quality jobs and reduce energy consumption. reducing energy consumption, together with energy efficiency, is a quick and effective way of tackling many problems such as energy security, dependence on foreign sources, high prices and unemployment. eliminating unnecessary consumption through better efficiency, stronger connectivity, greater market integration and sustainable investment in energy, in particular in buildings, could allow households to access a single, affordable, competitive and secure energy market on equal terms and avoid energy poverty, which affected a quarter of eu citizens in 2012.
for the s&d group. mr. editor, i want to thank you for your very good cooperation. our current way of life, the functioning of our economy and indeed our entire modern society are completely dependent on an uninterrupted supply of available energy, both in price and in physical form. energy security is therefore naturally one of our top priorities. not only will action by the member states be very important, but action by the european union will also play an increasingly important role. that is why we need an effective and strong european strategy to meet our energy needs in the future. a strategy that is not just a repetition of traditional recipes for our energy problems. the view has long prevailed among experts and the public that energy security is limited to the search for access to new fossil fuels, in particular oil and natural gas. thus, discussions often turned to plans for new gas and oil pipelines. this view was based on a century-long dependence on these raw materials. i believe that this attitude is long overdue. our long-term energy security is threatened today by our unsustainable, even irrational, dependence on oil and gas. it is not just imports from countries that are prone to use the so-called energy weapon to advance their foreign policy objectives. i also see a threat in the uncritical support of unconventional mining ... (the president cut off the speaker) the technologies used today have a clear negative impact on the health of citizens and the quality of the environment. this alone should be enough to ban fracking in the european union. that's not the only reason. the great danger is also that it will only prolong our dependence on oil and gas. the extraction of these unconventional resources will only postpone the much-needed transition to a low-carbon economy. that is why our group is tabled an amendment calling on the member states to stop extracting unconventional resources by hydraulic fracturing in europe. i am very pleased that the report presented is not limited to a short-sighted attempt to push for the construction of new oil and gas pipelines or to find more reliable partners. on the contrary, it offers very specific proposals and measures to gradually reduce our dependence and, in the process, to strengthen the competitiveness of our economy. the european energy security strategy must start first and foremost at home, in the european union. we need to fundamentally change the way we use energy, or in other words, the way we waste it. energy conservation is one of the least costly ways to enhance our energy security. lower consumption also means less dependence on oil and gas imports. it is regrettable that this is the area where member states did not have greater ambition last autumn and did not adopt a higher binding target for energy efficiency.

rapporteur.– madam president, i welcome the opportunity here to present a report which has already been adopted by the committee on international trade (inta), with contributions from the committee on the internal market and consumer protection (imco) and the committee on development (deve). the report looks into the european union’s common commercial policy and its impact on so-called public—private partnerships (ppps). as everybody knows, ppps are arrangements where the public sector and private sector act together in order to deliver certain types of services of general interest to the public. those services could be, for instance, infrastructure, like roads, public transport, power plants or water treatment plants. they could also be some kind of social services, like health care or education. last, but not least, in recent years, they could be realised in the field of innovative high-tech sectors. what is important to stress is that they are not current practice in well—developed countries, but they are becoming more and more important and widely used by donors in developing countries. ppp projects account for roughly 15% to 20% of total infrastructure investments in those countries. the report concentrates mainly on two aspects of ppp projects. one is, of course, the eu’s own interests, which means promotion of eu trade interests. participating in ppp projects provides eu companies with a great opportunity to grow and to gain new markets, if we take into account the current market conditions, slow economic recovery and the remaining high levels of unemployment in europe. we can all agree, i hope, that european companies can achieve growth only if they go international and enter other non-european markets. therefore, we have to build success stories, models and good practices concerning ppps to encourage our companies to go there. we also have to create things like one-stop shops or user-friendly platforms. we should use the good experiences of institutions already engaged in those projects, like the european investment bank and others. at the same time there is another goal, namely pursuing our development agenda. this is a crucial point. i think that we can create synergies with our development objectives by pursuing ppp projects. we all know that massive investments are required in developing countries in terms of infrastructure, energy supply or access to water. a substantial part of this funding will need to come from the private sector, where ppp can play a crucial role. of course we also have bad examples, particularly in some developing countries where ppps were in trouble. there were badly designed projects, engineering problems, too much bureaucracy, delays in realisation and poor project management. that is also why it is so important to work towards a common approach to tackling all those challenges. i think that this report could play a positive role in that. this report, i need to stress, does not make any attempt to establish new legislation or bureaucracy or anything like that. it just urges the eu institutions to take the necessary steps on the existing playing field to promote the participation of eu companies in ppp projects. it has been prepared in a spirit of very good cooperation between the political groups and committees. i hope that it will be received as well by the plenary of the european parliament.

projects in the public interest, notably in the infrastructure sector or other capital-intensive sectors. secondly, that cooperation between the private and public sectors can foster innovation, research and development through increased competition. thirdly, the importance of facilitating the participation of smes in public—private partnerships. finally, ppps give opportunities abroad, which can increase european companies’ market access in government procurement in countries outside the eu and redress the asymmetry between eu and other countries’ levels of openness in government in writing. the draft eu milk and milk products sector outlook report review of the implementation of the milk and milk products package deals primarily with the implementation of the milk and milk products package (the 'milk package') which is valid from 3 october 2012 to 30 june 2020. the report notes that milk producers are particularly vulnerable to market and price fluctuations. the current situation is negatively affected by the russian embargo. the milk package has reportedly a low level of implementation. the report recommends that the potential of long-term contracts be used more fully. it also proposes that more use be made of promotional measures and that the protected designation of origin and geographical indication be better treated. the report also stresses that the current measures of the ten-t safety net, such as public intervention and private storage, are not sufficient and calls on the european commission to introduce additional safeguard measures. i therefore voted in favour of the report without hesitation, because it is in the interest of the czech citizens that the european commission take further action to stabilise the milk market.
in writing. on 31 march 2015, after 30 years, the eu ended the milk quota regime, posing a major challenge to the entire milk and milk products sector, which is characterised by price volatility, high demand for milk on the market, but also by the complicated situation of primary producers. the european parliament recommended a number of measures to better manage the end of quotas and to increase the future competitiveness of the milk and milk products sector, to find new export markets and to improve technologies for sustainable production. in this respect, i would like to emphasise the role of the 2012 milk package, which strengthens contractual relations and the bargaining power of producers. its implementation has had a number of practical positive impacts, but only in those states that have given sufficient support to its implementation. many member states still have reservations. it is important that the commission adopts more favourable and realistic measures regarding the intervention price (not updated since 2008!), which must take more account of production costs. the commission will also be able to use the information provided by the member states to assess the impact of the measures taken on the milk market. the centre shall process market data and shall be able to send early warnings to the commission services, enabling it to act more rapidly in the early stages of a crisis in the sector. i am convinced that the importance of accurate and timely information will increase greatly in the post-quota period.
in writing. i supported today the report on the eu milk and milk products outlook review of the implementation of the milk and milk products package, as it can help to improve the difficult situation of milk producers who may be affected by large fluctuations in milk prices or high energy costs, for example. it is also important to address this issue at european level and thus contribute effectively to the interests of czech farmers. the adoption of the report was recommended by the ministry of agriculture of the czech republic.

in writing. ‒ the existing fruit and vegetable regime is too complex and unfortunately does not provide legal certainty. i therefore believe that the first step in making producer organisations more attractive should be to simplify the regime and remove legal uncertainty, which is why i voted in favour of the draft report. the fruit and vegetables sector, with its size, accounts for 0,98% of the total arable land area of the czech republic and has been experiencing a sustained slight decline, which needs to be changed. the association of the czech producer sector, which can be traced back to 1998, when the first sales cooperative with a territorial scope covering the whole of the czech republic was established, showed the possibility of improving its market position. at the time of the czech republic's accession to the eu, the sector's organisation was around 20%, but by 2007 it had already reached 28,5%. at present, the organization rate is almost 40%. the area of fruit and vegetable market gardens included in producer organisations and producer groups in the czech republic now totals 9 638 ha (an increase of 27.2% compared to 2007) and represents almost 39% of the total area of production fruit and vegetable market gardens in the agricultural sector in the czech republic, which totals 25,2 thousand ha. this is an important issue and i hope that this draft report is a step forward.
in writing. the reform of the fruit and vegetables regime implemented in 2007 confirmed and extended the policy of strengthening the role of producer organisations and associations of producer organisations. this is particularly important in the fruit and vegetables sector, where the union has essentially left the market free. eu financial support targeted at producer organisations is targeted at 4,1% of the value of marketed production. the share of the total value of marketed fruit and vegetables produced by producer organisations increased to 43% in 2010, but there are still large differences in the degree of organisation of producers between member states and in a number of countries fruit and vegetable producers still have a very weak position in the distribution chain. nevertheless, like the rapporteur, i believe that the increase in the degree of producer organisation so far is evidence of the success of the eu's policy of encouraging the creation and development of producer organisations. further improvements in this area should remain one of the eu priorities for the fruit and vegetables regime. for this reason, i support strengthening incentives for the creation of producer organisations and associations of producer organisations and for their merger. it is important to find a way to make membership in these organisations more attractive; the first step to this should be to simplify the regime and improve the management of producer organisations.

in writing. - i have been following the negotiations on the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip) closely for several months, and i was therefore not at all indifferent to the outcome of the vote on wednesday. based on the information available or leaked, my concerns about the future of europe and its citizens grew and the approved proposal did not give me much hope. i had hoped for a much greater emphasis on protecting workers' rights, the environment and health. instead, i was greeted with empty phrases and promises that the european union would not lower its standards. most seem to believe that europe has such great negotiators that the us will give us a pass on everything and nothing will change for the eu, except that we will have a more fluid transatlantic trade that we will all benefit from. i no longer trust the judgment of the european representatives and i fear that they have lost their vision of a happy future, which has been implanted in them by the multinational corporations. i disagree with ttip not only as a trade agreement, but also as a geopolitical agreement, as it is increasingly being called. i reject the notion that europe and the united states must work hand in hand to create an economic giant that will at least try to dominate the world again and prevent the rise of china and other global players. ttip is a treaty of fear, and that's why i voted against the proposal.
in writing. ‒ today we voted on the ttip transatlantic trade and investment partnership. its purported aim is to remove barriers to trade so that it is easier to buy and sell goods and services between the eu and the us. but what are these obstacles? differences in the laws, technical regulations, standards and approval procedures. the agreement aims, among other things, to get as close as possible to the elimination of all tariffs on transatlantic trade in industrial and agricultural products, the european commission says. so we're going to accept american genetically modified corn? the agreement also includes investment protection. however, it also involves arbitration of disputes between the investor and the state, excluding the state courts. among other things, the state is to be responsible for labour disputes under national law i.e. for trade union strikes and demonstrations. they must compensate the investor for the damage caused by these disputes. regardless of their legitimacy. another problem with ttip is the need for consensus on intellectual property rights, where the european and american models differ greatly and a separate chapter is the regulation of personal data protection. the proceedings are held behind closed doors. no one has invited, for example, representatives of european trade unions, nor are the voices of citizens who are agitating against the agreement being heard. i'm saying this deal is only good for one side, and it's not good for europe. i voted against it.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the recommendation on ttip not only because i support the negotiation of the agreement, but also because the ep expressed some views in it that should lead to a better ttip agreement. the old investor-state dispute settlement (isds) mechanism should be replaced by a new system with publicly appointed and independent judges, public hearings and an appeal mechanism. i welcome that. in my experience, i consider that a welcome development. the new isds should ensure greater predictability, independence and impartiality of decision-making. a safeguard clause should also be included in the ttip agreement to apply in the event of an increase in imports of a product which would pose a risk of serious damage to domestic food production. the european parliament has voted today to overcome ideological differences and take a major step towards a better and more inclusive ttip. i also thank the colleagues who supported the agreement.
in writing. ‒ the resolution adopted by parliament is intended to rectify in part the too benevolent mandate given to the european commission by the member states. it is essential to stress, however, that this is a non-legislative resolution, a recommendation to the european commission, not a vote on ttip itself. the resolution aims to highlight areas where no compromise can be made and where european standards must be accepted. it would be irresponsible to favour populism when it is still possible to intervene in the negotiations. the european parliament is the only democratically elected body of the eu, and therefore has the responsibility to outline what agreement it will or will not accept. for example, not adopting the resolution would imply tacit support for the original isds and for another problematic part of the agreement. the resolution is the result of months of cooperation involving 14 committees. it is not a perfect text, but it does give a clear indication of what the commission should focus on in the further negotiations. for example, parliament has set hard limits on data protection and financial services and rejected any form of private arbitration under isds. in my view, the report could have contained more recommendations on the environment, health and food, but as i have already said, this is a compromise, which is simply the best that this parliament could have agreed on by a majority. but this is by no means a green light for ttip as such.
‒ it is certainly true that the eu needs a better trade agreement with the us. it is also true, however, that such a contract must reflect both commercial interests and the interests of citizens, particularly in the area of health and consumer protection. the draft report by s&d mep bernard lange was withdrawn from the june plenary session, as a number of right-wing meps had clearly stated in advance that they would reject the report if they accepted the social democrats' demand for the exclusion of the system of investor-state dispute settlement in the form of private arbitration (isds), as there were legitimate concerns about the disadvantageous position of states vis-à-vis private companies. the eu president, martin schulz, therefore proposed a compromise proposal, which won the support of the majority of social democrats, in the new negotiations, and which calls for the replacement of the isds mechanism, i.e. the mechanism of private arbitrations, by a new, public, democratic and more transparent mechanism. i am pleased that the european parliament, thanks to my vote, supported both the compromise proposal on the dispute settlement mechanism and the entire document. i consider this to be a clearly positive step in the process of further negotiation of a treaty that is unquestionably very necessary for the eu's competitiveness on a global scale. the european parliament will of course vote on the final text of the treaty and all the proposed measures will certainly be subject to detailed scrutiny.
in writing. i supported the resolution on ttip by the rapporteur, mr lange, because it gives a great deal of clarity to the political mandate and demands of the socialist members of the european parliament towards the negotiators of the agreement. today's vote does not automatically mean acceptance of the final text of the agreement, which is still being negotiated. the european parliament has made clear today the specific points without which it will not support the final agreement. these include, for example, the exclusion of public services, ensuring the protection of workers, the environment or respecting regulations on product safety and consumer rights.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report containing the european parliament's recommendations to the commission on the negotiations on the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip) in particular because ttip will ensure a level playing field for member states' investors and in particular an attractive eu for foreign investment, which is a major contributor to our economic growth and employment. ttip aims to facilitate trade and investment between the two parties.

in writing. on 8 july 2015, we voted on the report by sergio cofferati on the proposal for a directive amending directive 2007/36/ec as regards the promotion of long-term shareholder engagement and directive 2013/34/eu as regards certain elements of the corporate governance statement. the revision mainly concerns the management and administration of companies. in particular, it is intended to increase shareholders' incentives to become more voluntarily involved in the companies in which they have invested by buying shares. the debate on the proposal in the rapporteurs' negotiations was very complex from the outset. the original draft report was of a very high quality and contained a number of provisions which were important to our group, but which the rapporteur gradually reduced in importance during the discussions in order to please the right-wing groups in particular. however, with the help of the votes of other smaller groups, we were finally able to vote on the key points in the committee, such as the country by country reporting and the adjustment of the remuneration of company bodies. that is why i have finally decided to support this report in the plenary.
in writing. the cofferati report concerns a proposal to revise two directives in the field of commercial law, which govern the management and administration of companies and are intended in particular to encourage shareholders to be involved in the long-term affairs of the companies in which they have invested. the financial crisis has shown that shareholders have in many cases encouraged managers to take excessive short-term risks with a focus on short-term returns. the proposed measures are expected to affect approximately 10 000 listed companies in europe. despite the complexity of the negotiations and the many concessions made in the search for a compromise, the report managed to incorporate a number of important positive elements, the most important being the so-called country by country reporting, which would help to combat tax evasion, as well as the first attempt to regulate remuneration at european level. that is why i decided to support the report in the final vote.
in writing. - i supported the report because it contains useful changes leading to an improvement in the position of shareholders and greater transparency of public limited companies. 0 other on the contrary, i am disappointed that the report includes public disclosure of company profits and the publication of tax rulings, in addition to the commission's original proposal. i think that is bad to that extent and i hope that the amendment will not enter into force in that form. the adjustment of tax rulings to increase transparency and the introduction of cbcr by firms needs to be done in such a way that the objectives of these measures are achieved at reasonable cost and without jeopardising the competitive position of european firms. it is much more appropriate to deal with this systematically in the tax reports which are now being prepared by the econ committee and the taxe subcommittee, where i would like to support a well-reasoned proposal.
in writing. the report by rapporteur sergio gaetano cofferati represents a major shift in the field of entrepreneurship and transparency. i voted for it mainly because it offers a solution to combat tax evasion and avoidance. it requires large corporations and public interest groups to submit annual financial reports in the country where they are active. i welcome the fact that large companies will have to disclose to the public information about the number of employees, the size of turnover, profits, subsidies, but especially the tax on profits or losses. i am convinced that this approach will help to prevent disasters like luxleaks and contribute to a fairer distribution of wealth in europe. in the context of the current financial and economic instability in the european union, it is abundantly clear that we cannot tolerate the practice of circumventing tax and other laws. i voted in favour of a provision which encourages greater and long-term shareholder involvement in the management of listed companies. i believe that the long-term involvement of these entities will help to stabilise the situation on the financial market. today, investors are often driven by the idea of getting rich quick, but that does not have such long-term economic benefits. i also voted for more control over the remuneration of company board members. it is time for sustainability policy to finally play a crucial role in the distribution of the generous remuneration of managers.
in writing. ‒ i am pleased that the european parliament has adopted by a very strong majority the report by the social democratic rapporteur cofferati, which aims in particular to promote the role of shareholders in large companies. parliament sent a clear message that companies and companies listed on stock exchanges should publish all information on profits made, income taxes and public subsidies received in each country. in many eu countries, this is still largely untreated and non-transparent. the proposed amendment to the shareholder rights directive also includes proposals to ensure that listed companies will be able to identify their shareholders, asset managers and institutional investors such as pension funds or insurance companies. we have included in the draft directive the requirement that shareholders be able to vote every three years on the remuneration policy of the company's management, which i believe can have an impact on the more responsible and efficient behaviour of their managers and their orientation towards the long-term prosperity of the company. however, member states will be free to decide whether this vote is decisive or merely advisory. the proposal also includes measures to combat tax evasion and avoidance, in particular for multinational enterprises, but also for public-interest entities such as insurance companies. they will have to report openly on the losses, profits and taxes reported in each country where they operate.
in writing. ‒ in line with my agenda on better regulation, i supported the report on long-term shareholder engagement. the report aims at encouraging long-term shareholder engagement as a way to contribute to the long-term sustainability of eu companies, but also to create an attractive environment for shareholders. i am in favour of full transparency and disclosure of information that can be beneficial for shareholders; however, rules we establish should not be too detailed and put a disproportionate burden on businesses. i opposed the provisions on submitting the remuneration policy to a vote and imposing a set ratio between directors’ pay and employees’ salaries. such requirements would impose a high administrative burden on the businesses while they are of a minimum benefit for the markets and the shareholders; today shareholders already have the right to ask for this information during the general meeting.
in writing. ‒ in my view, the focus should be on long-term objectives, which should encourage greater shareholder involvement in the future. it is important to have a dialogue with them on business matters. another no less important aspect is transparency, which i believe should apply to the activities of larger companies, particularly with regard to profits made, taxes on profits and subsidies received. this form is necessary to ensure the confidence of shareholders and other companies in the eu trading sphere.
in writing. i supported the compromise resulting from the trilogue between the ep, the commission and the council. it includes the creation of a market stability reserve as of 1 january 2019 and an exemption for the so-called solidarity allowances allocated annually to new member states, which will be withdrawn from the market stability reserve until 2025. i know that compromise was born with difficulty, there has been a blocking minority in the council for a long time, and that is why i am glad that a solution has finally been adopted which will allow the situation on the emissions market to be unblocked and it will be able to fulfil its purpose once again, namely to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in an economically efficient way. at the same time, i'm glad that the future of the ems is coming to the table. a delayed response to a weakening of the system is not good for the economy. it penalizes responsible and long-term thinking and rewards speculation or irresponsible resource management.
‒ there is no doubt that the current system for regulating greenhouse gas emissions has not met the expectations that were placed in it and that it needs to be significantly reformed. i am pleased that the european parliament has supported the introduction of a mechanism called the market stability reserve, which should stimulate investors to make sustainable investment decisions in the long term. the mechanism will be based on automatic transfer of allowances to reserves during periods of oversupply on the market and their release during periods of shortage. i consider a functioning and above all stable system of allowance trading based on high flexibility to be an essential part of the eu's climate policy and of sustainable economic growth in general. the legislative proposal adopted today is also favourable to the czech republic, as the final text includes compensation for the czech republic's loss of auction revenues. these outages are related to the earlier than expected deployment of the market stability reserve.
in writing. ‒ there are currently around 2 billion allowances remaining on the market. as we know, the effects of the economic crisis are behind this, but there are other factors as well. this fact has a negative impact not only on the auction price of the allowances themselves, but also on the incentives of operators to invest in more environmentally friendly measures. it is for this reason that i have decided to support the draft decision to create a market stability reserve. the reserve promises to significantly improve predictability and market stability and to provide incentives for investment in green innovation. as a consequence, emissions should also be gradually reduced. lastly, it will represent a welcome and, above all, desirable alignment between industrial and environmental policy today. in conclusion, i would like to say that i also appreciate the final form of this report in the context of the final negotiation on the content, which included compensatory clauses of importance to the czech republic.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on establishment of the market stability reserve for the emissions trading system. the emissions trading system was supposed to be an important step towards lowering the co2 emissions and was expected to serve as a best example of a system to fight against air pollution. but instead it became poorly functioning and led to a large surplus of allowances. establishment of the market stability reserve should help to tackle the over-supply of allowances and to find a better balance within the ets. in trialogue the european parliament and council agreed on the start date for the msr (2019, two years earlier than proposed by the commission) and on placing the ‘backloaded’ allowances directly into the msr. i agree with this review and i hope this step will help to bring about a well-functioning system incentivising innovation and the competitiveness of our industry.
in writing. ‒ i am personally sceptical that further administrative adjustment will resolve and stabilise the allowance system in the long term. the problem lies in the system of the artificially created market itself. i am convinced that, despite the pre-defined rules for intervention in the allowance market, the system is not sustainable in the long term. moreover, i have reservations about the administrative intervention itself, which may be very dangerous economically for many businesses in the future. i agree with the rapporteur that the commission needs to have a fundamental discussion on the reallocation of free allowances, but i also recommend that the very essence of the ets be addressed.
in writing. ‒ i have always been against the introduction of emission allowances, which put european businesses at a disadvantage in global competition, but once they have been introduced, the rules must be respected and the system must not be constantly tampered with. i reject the creation of a market stabilisation reserve to regulate the supply of auctioned allowances, and i also reject the practice of so-called backloading of emission allowances, which i regard as non-systemic market intervention that will only artificially affect the price and will lead to a deterioration in the competitiveness of industry. the eu must wake up from the illusions of zero emissions, full decarbonisation and 100% renewable energy.
in writing. ‒ i fully supported the commission proposal and the corresponding european parliament position. until now, the workers’ rights for seafarers varied from one member state to another. i believe that considering the challenges faced by the maritime sector, especially labour shortages, harmonizing seafarers’ rights across the eu is an important step to take. both access to information and consultation rights are fundamental rights and should be guaranteed for off-shore and on-shore workers. ensuring a level playing field between workers in the fisheries and shipping sectors would result also in fairer competition.
in writing. ‒ as a shadow rapporteur i gave my consent to the agreement on scientific cooperation between the eu and switzerland within horizon 2020 and iter activities. switzerland gained the status of ‘associated country’ in 2004. this status enabled its participation in the eu’s sixth research framework programme, seventh rfp and the eighth framework programme horizon 2020. however, switzerland held a referendum to reintroduce immigration quotas in february 2014, which had repercussions on the other agreements, notably on the agreement on the scientific cooperation within the eu framework programmes. a new agreement between the eu and switzerland was reached during the negotiations in 2014, granting switzerland ‘associated country’ status in some parts of horizon 2020 (excellent science, nuclear energy research) until the end of 2016 in exchange for a financial contribution. i agree with a need to join the effort in the field of science and to extend this cooperation also to another countries. therefore i support this agreement.
in writing. on 8 july 2015, we voted on the report on the proposal for a council decision on guidelines for the employment policies of the member states. the treaty on the functioning of the european union provides that member states consider their economic policies and employment promotion to be a matter of common interest and therefore coordinate their action within the council. the commission's proposal includes reforming education systems to match skills to labour market demands, modernising social security systems, reforming the pension system, including the correlation between retirement age and life expectancy, and shifting the tax burden from labour to other sources of taxation that are less harmful to employment and growth. in general, the agea report was much better than the commission's original proposal, as it also contains, among other things, references to decent working conditions and adequate wages, references to adequate social protection, including a guaranteed minimum income, and a reference to the importance of addressing the growing shortage of workers in the public sector, such as health care and social services. however, the final text of the report was strongly affected by the proposals of the ppe and alde colleagues and was therefore significantly weakened, especially as regards the social security adjustment. that's why i was forced to stay.
in writing. the european parliament adopted, in the context of the consultation process, amendments to the text of the draft council decision on the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states. it has thus amended the original proposal of the european commission in an attempt to make it even more effective, in particular by strengthening the social and environmental dimensions of the text. i believe that, in view of the unemployment rate in the eu and the growing number of people living in poverty (today, it is estimated that there are some 20 million people), it is essential to establish reliable poverty indicators and to continue to fight against all forms of poverty and discrimination, with a focus on extreme poverty. the interconnectedness of member states' economies and labour markets is a fact across the eu, and we therefore call for decisive, coordinated, ambitious and effective policy action at both union and national level. in this regard, there is a need to strengthen investment, in particular in the development of smes, micro-enterprises, innovative start-ups and enterprises that promote green employment.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of these guidelines which ask for more specific actions to reduce unemployment and support job creation by smes. on one side, labour demand must be boosted, especially for young people, and on the other side we need to ensure the labour offer matches the need of the european businesses. on the job creation side, i supported all provisions which intend to cut red tape for smes to hire people. on education and training, i am in favour of measures to enhance the entrepreneurship skills of the european workforce and measures enabling it to diversify its skills and so better adapt to a fast-changing labour market. more specifically, to tackle youth unemployment, i supported the overall strategy to consistently implement the youth guarantee at national level. eu funding should be targeted to improve their skills and assist them throughout the starting up of their own businesses, with better access to information and funding. i opposed provisions on setting up a union minimum wage in the eu as it is a regulatory competence of the member states.

in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament resolution on the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund following the 568 redundancies which occurred in broadcom communications in finland. these redundancies are the result of a larger trend affecting the finnish electronics industry and hurt a region which already was affected by nokia redundancies in the past. the finnish assistance to the workers complies with all criteria for the use of the european globalisation adjustment fund and consists of three measures: helping workers transfer to a new job, helping them start their own business and providing them with appropriate training.
in writing. on 8 july 2015, i abstained from the vote on the report on the mandate for the trialogue on the draft budget for the financial year 2016. this report is intended to set out the mandate for the european parliament team's negotiations with the council on the 2016 budget. the draft eu budget for 2016 provides for an amount of eur 153,5 billion in commitment appropriations, including eur 4,5 billion from the 2014 surplus. this represents an overall increase of 2,4% in commitment appropriations. in the negotiations on the 2016 mandate, our group has made some partial successes with its amendments, for example on the integration of the requirement to create decent and quality jobs and to increase employment and the development of enterprises and entrepreneurship. despite these partial victories, however, the main aspects of the mandate remain the same as in previous years. thus, the emphasis on austerity, the channelling of the eu and its citizens into the service of large multinational corporations, and the apparent support of their financial interests has been maintained. but the current wording of the mandate is arguably the best wording in the last decade, because even the most entrenched european institutions have finally begun to admit the many mistakes they made in previous years, but it is still not enough, which is why i had to abstain.
